42104.q: A steel mill's smoke harms nearby households. Which classification is most precise?
options: Negative production externality
Negative consumption externality
Positive production externality
Positive consumption externality
42104.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
42104.feedback: Production imposes a third-party cost. Because the smoke is created during production, the omitted harm raises marginal social cost above the mill's private marginal cost.

42105.q: Secondhand smoke from using a product harms restaurant patrons. What kind of spillover is this?
options: Negative production externality
Negative consumption externality
Positive production externality
Positive consumption externality
42105.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
42105.feedback: The harmful spillover follows consumption. The purchase itself is not the spillover; the harm generated when the product is consumed falls on people outside the transaction.

42106.q: A beekeeper's hives improve nearby orchard yields without payment. How is the effect classified?
options: Negative production externality
Negative consumption externality
Positive production externality
Positive consumption externality
42106.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
42106.feedback: Production by the beekeeper creates an external benefit. The beekeeper does not capture all of the added orchard output, so the social benefit of producing hives exceeds the private benefit.

42107.q: A vaccination reduces infection risk for people other than the patient. What is the spillover?
options: Negative consumption externality
Negative production externality
Positive production externality
Positive consumption externality
42107.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
42107.feedback: Consuming the vaccination benefits third parties. The patient receives a private benefit, while reduced transmission creates an additional social benefit for other people.

42108.q: A landscaping company creates noise while serving a customer. Which channel creates the externality?
options: Production
Consumption
A public-good channel
A price-control channel
42108.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
42108.feedback: The spillover is created while the service is produced. The customer and landscaper are the transacting parties, while nearby residents experience a cost created by the production process.

42109.q: A driver's use of a congested road delays other drivers. Which description is best?
options: A positive production externality
A negative consumption externality
A private cost borne only by the driver
A positive consumption externality
42109.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
42109.feedback: Road use imposes delay on other users. Each trip adds congestion delays for other road users, so the driver's private cost understates the social cost of road use.

42118.q: A rule requires factories to install a verified scrubber. What policy type is this?
options: A corrective consumer subsidy
A tradable-permit market
Command-and-control technology regulation
A private Coase bargain
42118.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
42118.feedback: The rule mandates a technology. Because the regulator specifies the equipment rather than a price or emissions allowance, firms cannot choose a different compliance technology.

42119.q: A city caps each plant's sulfur emissions at 20 tons. What instrument is used?
options: A consumption subsidy
An unregulated permit market
A price floor on output
An emissions standard
42119.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
42119.feedback: A legal maximum emissions amount is a standard. The legal maximum directly constrains each plant's emissions quantity; it does not create a subsidy or a tradable right by itself.

42132.q: Education benefits employers and neighbors beyond the student. What quantity tendency can result?
options: Underconsumption relative to social optimum
Overconsumption
No efficiency effect
A binding price floor
42132.commonError: Reversing social and private curves or predicting overproduction instead of underproduction.
42132.feedback: Private marginal benefit can lie below social marginal benefit. Because consumers count only their private return, MPB lies below MSB and the private market stops before all socially worthwhile units are consumed.

42134.q: A per-unit subsidy equals vaccination's marginal external benefit. What is intended?
options: Reduce vaccination below market quantity
Leave private incentives unchanged
Increase vaccination toward socially efficient quantity
Turn benefit into external cost
42134.commonError: Confusing subsidy expenditure with external benefit or taxing a positive externality.
42134.feedback: The subsidy raises private incentive by the external benefit. By rewarding the external benefit, the subsidy raises the consumer's effective private incentive and moves the MPB-based choice toward the MSB-based efficient quantity.

options: Drivers share congestion costs imposed on one another

P77-MFAIL-M-006.feedback: When each driver considers the private benefit of the trip but not the congestion delay imposed on other drivers, road use can exceed the socially efficient level.

42110.q: What distinguishes an external cost from an ordinary private cost?
options: It is always paid as a tax
It is any expense a seller records
An external cost falls on a third party outside the transaction
It exists only for public goods
42110.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
42110.feedback: External effects reach people outside the exchange. Costs already paid by the buyer or seller are private; an external cost is omitted from their exchange and therefore from the market price.

42111.q: Why does the sign of an externality not reveal its production or consumption channel?
options: Sign and channel are always the same
Only production creates positive spillovers
Only consumption creates negative spillovers
Sign identifies harm or benefit; channel identifies which activity creates it
42111.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
42111.feedback: Sign and source are separate dimensions. A positive or negative sign identifies the effect on third parties, whereas production or consumption identifies the activity that generates it.

42112.q: A firm's research helps other firms imitate a process. Which private-social relationship is likely?
options: Social benefit of production exceeds the producer's private benefit
Social cost of consumption exceeds private cost
Private benefit of consumption exceeds social benefit
The effect is negative because rivals benefit
42112.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
42112.feedback: Knowledge spillovers can make social production returns exceed private returns. Because imitators receive gains without compensating the innovator, private production incentives can be weaker than the total social return.

42113.q: Buyers receive all benefits and sellers bear all costs of a trade. What externality evidence is present?
options: A negative production externality
None from those facts alone
A positive consumption externality
Both positive and negative externalities
42113.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
42113.feedback: An externality requires a third-party effect. Benefits and costs confined to the transacting parties are already private; evidence of a spillover requires an effect on someone else.

42114.q: A factory ignores a constant marginal pollution cost. Relative to efficient quantity, what does the market tend to produce?
options: Too little output
The efficient output automatically
Too much output
Zero output in every case
42114.commonError: Using private curves alone when social costs or benefits determine efficiency.
42114.feedback: Ignoring external cost makes private marginal cost too low. The factory compares MPB with MPC and omits pollution damage, so MPC lies below MSC and the private intersection occurs at too much output.

42115.q: Consumers ignore harms their purchases impose on bystanders. What is the usual quantity result?
options: Underconsumption
No quantity distortion
A shortage caused by a price ceiling
Overconsumption
42115.commonError: Using private curves alone when social costs or benefits determine efficiency.
42115.feedback: Private marginal benefit exceeds social marginal benefit. When consumers omit harm to bystanders, MPB lies above MSB and the market chooses units whose social benefit is below their social cost.

42120.q: Plants have different abatement costs, but a regulator orders equal cuts. What concern arises?
options: The same aggregate reduction may cost more than necessary
The policy changes a negative externality into a positive one
Equal cuts guarantee equal marginal costs
The rule automatically creates tax revenue
42120.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
42120.feedback: Uniform cuts can ignore marginal-cost differences. Equal cuts ignore differences in marginal abatement cost, so the target could be reached with less total cost by shifting reductions toward lower-cost plants.

42121.q: A safety rule bans disposal of toxic waste in a river. What is its intended mechanism?
options: Subsidize river disposal
Prevent the harmful action rather than price each unit
Create a tradable cap automatically
Guarantee compensation to every resident
42121.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
42121.feedback: A prohibition directly restricts the action. A ban is a direct quantity restriction: it prevents the damaging behavior instead of charging a price for each unit of harm.

42124.q: How does an emissions standard differ from a corrective tax?
options: A standard fixes a legal quantity constraint; a tax sets a price on harm
A standard creates revenue while a tax never does
A tax fixes emissions with certainty
They are identical whenever enforced
42124.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
42124.feedback: Quantity and price instruments use different control variables. A standard determines an allowed quantity, while a corrective tax changes the marginal private price; those instruments need not produce identical certainty or revenue.

42125.q: Why might a performance standard be preferred to mandated technology?
options: It removes monitoring needs
It can let firms choose how to meet the required outcome
It guarantees zero compliance cost
It turns the externality into a public good
42125.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
42125.feedback: Performance standards preserve some compliance flexibility. Firms retain freedom to select the least-cost method, although regulators still must define, monitor, and enforce the performance outcome.

42128.q: A corrective tax equals marginal external cost at efficient output. What does it accomplish?
options: It makes the decision-maker face the omitted social cost
It guarantees sellers bear the legal tax
It eliminates distributional effects
It makes revenue equal DWL
42128.commonError: Confusing the corrective wedge, incidence, revenue, and deadweight loss.
42128.feedback: The tax internalizes marginal external cost. At the efficient quantity, adding the tax to the private margin closes the gap between private and social cost and removes the incentive to choose harmful excess units.

42129.q: Why is tax revenue not the same as deadweight loss?
options: Revenue is always larger than social costs
Revenue is a transfer; deadweight loss is forgone net social surplus
Deadweight loss is a producer transfer
They are identical with downward demand
42129.commonError: Confusing the corrective wedge, incidence, revenue, and deadweight loss.
42129.feedback: Transfers and efficiency losses differ. Tax revenue changes who holds purchasing power, while deadweight loss measures mutually beneficial surplus that disappears because quantity is inefficient.

42133.q: Why can a positive production externality make output too low?
options: MPC exceeds every buyer's willingness to pay
Producers do not receive the full social benefit they create
Consumers impose an external cost
MSC is always above MPC
42133.commonError: Reversing social and private curves or predicting overproduction instead of underproduction.
42133.feedback: Omitted external benefits weaken private incentives. For a positive production externality, MSC lies below MPC because some production benefit reaches third parties rather than the producer.

42135.q: Why is subsidy expenditure not proof that a positive-externality policy raises welfare?
options: Every subsidy is equal DWL
Spending determines externality sign
A subsidy cannot change quantity
Correction benefits must be compared with resource and financing costs
42135.commonError: Confusing subsidy expenditure with external benefit or taxing a positive externality.
42135.feedback: Fiscal cost and net social benefit are distinct. Government spending is a fiscal cost, not a direct measure of welfare; policy evaluation must compare the external benefit gained with real resource and financing costs.

42136.q: A regulator issues permits covering exactly 1,000 tons. What fixes aggregate emissions?
options: The total number of valid permits
The number of firms trading
Initial market shares
Tax revenue from trades
42136.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
42136.feedback: The permit total fixes the cap. Each permit authorizes a unit of emissions, so the number of valid permits fixes total legal emissions even when ownership changes through trade.

42137.q: Firm A abates for $20 per ton and B for $70. At a $45 permit price, what is efficient?
options: B abates more because its cost is higher
A abates more and can sell permits; B buys permits and abates less
Both must abate equally
Trading loosens the cap
42137.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
42137.feedback: The lower-cost reducer abates when cost is below permit price. Firm A's $20 abatement cost is below the $45 permit price, while Firm B's $70 cost is above it, so trade assigns more reduction to the lower-cost source.

42138.q: What happens to the emissions cap when two firms trade an existing permit?
options: It rises by one unit
It falls by one unit
The cap is unchanged
It becomes voluntary
42138.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
42138.feedback: Trading reallocates an existing right. A trade transfers permission to emit from one firm to another; it neither creates nor retires a permit and therefore leaves aggregate emissions unchanged.

42148.q: A paper mill buys downstream fishing rights and cuts pollution because it bears lost fishery value. What is illustrated?
options: Business integration internalizes the spillover
A binding price ceiling
A government permit cap
Guaranteed correction through norms
42148.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
42148.feedback: Common ownership brings the external cost into private calculation. Combining ownership makes the mill bear both production gains and fishery losses, bringing a previously external cost into the same private decision.

P52B-MFAIL-H-001.q: At the next unit of a competitive product, a buyer values it at $18, the producer uses $14 of resources, and pollution harms neighbors by $6. Which outcome does a $6 per-unit tax encourage?
options: Forgo the unit: private gains are $4 but net social benefit is -$2.
Produce the unit: the $4 private gain measures its full social benefit.
Produce the unit: $6 of tax revenue makes its net social benefit $4.
Forgo the unit: every taxed unit has zero social benefit.
P52B-MFAIL-H-001.commonError: Treating a corrective tax as unrelated to marginal incentives.
P52B-MFAIL-H-001.feedback: The trade has a private gain of 18 - 14 = $4, but net social benefit is 18 - 14 - 6 = -$2. A $6 tax makes the relevant private cost $20, above willingness to pay. Revenue is a transfer, not an extra resource benefit.

42117.q: Market quantity is 90, efficient quantity is 60, and marginal external cost is $8. What triangular DWL results?
42117.commonError: Using private curves alone when social costs or benefits determine efficiency.

42122.q: A plant saves $90 by evading one required emissions-control action. An inspection detects evasion with probability 0.20 and triggers a $300 fine. For a risk-neutral plant, which change would deter this evasion without changing the emissions standard?
options: Keep the current fine because $300 exceeds the $90 saving.
Reduce detection to 0.10 while retaining the $300 fine.
Raise the fine above $450 while keeping detection at 0.20.
Announce the same standard again without changing detection or penalties.
42122.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
42122.feedback: The expected penalty is 0.20 x 300 = $60, below the $90 saving. Deterrence requires 0.20 x fine > 90, or a fine above $450. A written standard alone does not change that comparison.

42123.q: A regulator knows the emissions target but not each firm's abatement cost. What design issue matters?
options: Every firm must have identical technology
Initial permit allocation determines the fixed cap
An output subsidy is required
Flexibility may reach the target at lower total cost
42123.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
42123.feedback: Flexibility can allocate reductions toward lower-cost sources. Flexibility lets low-cost firms undertake more abatement and high-cost firms less, potentially preserving the target while lowering total compliance cost.

42130.q: Before a corrective tax, a market sells 800 units. A $3 per-unit tax reduces sales to 500 units. What revenue is collected, and why does it differ from taxing the original sales volume?

$900, because only the 300 discouraged trades form the tax base.
$1,500, because the tax applies to the 500 units still traded.
$450, because revenue is the triangle over the quantity reduction.
42130.commonError: Confusing the corrective wedge, incidence, revenue, and deadweight loss.
42130.feedback: Post-tax revenue is 3 x 500 = $1,500. The forgone 300 units pay no tax. A welfare triangle and a revenue rectangle measure different things.

42131.q: Marginal external cost is $7, but corrective tax is $4. What wedge remains?

$11 per unit

42131.feedback: The remaining wedge is $7 - $4. The $4 tax internalizes only part of the $7 marginal harm, so decision-makers still omit $3 of social cost on each unit.

42139.q: A regulator retires 10% of outstanding permits. What changes directly?
options: The cap loosens
Only initial wealth changes
Abatement incentives disappear
The aggregate emissions cap tightens
42139.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
42139.feedback: Fewer permits authorize less emissions. Retiring permits reduces the legal quantity of emissions, requiring additional aggregate abatement if regulated demand for emissions is otherwise unchanged.

42140.q: Two plants must jointly reduce emissions by two tons. Each can remove at most one ton at each successive cost: Plant A, $20 then $30; Plant B, $60 then $90. With enforceable tradable permits and no trading costs, how should the two-ton reduction be allocated?
options: A removes both tons for $50, saving $30 relative to one ton each.
Each removes one ton for $80, because equal cuts minimize total cost.
B removes both tons for $150, because high-cost plants should abate first.
A removes one ton and B removes one for $50, because only the cheaper costs count.
42140.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
42140.feedback: The two cheapest feasible marginal reductions are A’s $20 and $30 tons: total $50. Equal cuts cost 20 + 60 = $80. Trading permits can reallocate abatement without changing the aggregate target.

42126.q: A production ban removes highly harmful and low-harm units. What tradeoff should be evaluated?
options: Only the regulator's budget
Whether tax incidence falls on buyers
Avoided external harm versus lost gains from low-harm output
Whether permit allocation is equal
42126.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
42126.feedback: Efficient regulation compares marginal social benefits and costs. Eliminating every unit can sacrifice trades whose private and social benefits still exceed their harm, so efficient policy compares marginal benefits and costs.

42127.q: A standard reaches the efficient pollution quantity but forces equal cuts despite unequal costs. Which assessment is accurate?
options: The target guarantees minimum total cost
Unequal costs make the target too strict
The standard is distributionally neutral
The target can be efficient while abatement allocation is not cost-effective
42127.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
42127.feedback: Outcome efficiency and least-cost allocation are distinct. Reaching the efficient aggregate quantity does not ensure least-cost abatement when marginal abatement costs remain unequal across firms.

42141.q: An enforceable permit cap is unchanged, but a new production opportunity raises demand for emissions. In a competitive permit market, price rises. A firm receives its permits free. Which response is consistent with cost minimization?
options: Ignore the price increase because freely allocated permits have no opportunity cost.
Reconsider abatement because using a free permit sacrifices a more valuable sale.
Increase total authorized emissions because higher demand automatically expands the cap.
Replace abatement with emissions because a higher permit price reduces the cost of using permits.
42141.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
42141.feedback: The fixed cap constrains total authorized emissions. Higher permit value raises the opportunity cost of surrendering a permit, even if its acquisition cost was zero, making additional abatement attractive at the margin.

42142.q: Permits are given free rather than auctioned. Which conclusion is sound?
options: Free allocation raises the cap
Auctioning creates more emissions
Allocation changes wealth but need not change cost-effective trading under frictionless competition
Initial allocation never affects distribution
42142.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
42142.feedback: Allocation affects distribution while the fixed cap governs total emissions. Free allocation changes who receives permit scarcity value, but with frictionless trading the cap and marginal-cost comparisons still govern total emissions and abatement.

42143.q: A permit system has a fixed cap but severe monitoring failures. What risk follows?
options: Monitoring guarantees lower costs
Permit price becomes a subsidy
Initial allocation repairs enforcement
Unrecorded emissions can exceed the legal cap
42143.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
42143.feedback: The cap requires enforceable emissions records. A cap is effective only when emissions are measured and permits are enforced; unrecorded emissions break the link between permits and actual pollution.

42144.q: A city tightens its permit cap with unchanged emissions demand. What likely happens?
options: Permits become scarcer and price tends to rise
Permits become abundant and price falls
The cap is unchanged
Marginal abatement cost becomes zero
42144.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
42144.feedback: A tighter cap reduces permit supply. With a smaller fixed supply of permits and unchanged demand to emit, scarcity increases and the equilibrium permit price tends to rise.

42146.q: Three firms can eliminate one ton for $15, $35, and $80. If two tons must be eliminated, what is minimum cost?
42146.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
42146.feedback: Choose the two lowest-cost reductions. Selecting the $15 and $35 reductions minimizes cost because the required two tons should be abated by the two lowest marginal-cost firms.

42149.q: A venue can cut nighttime noise at a $600 resource cost, preventing $1,000 of harm to nearby households. The venue has the right to operate. Households would also pay $100 to organize and enforce a contract. What payment range makes both sides strictly better off?
options: More than $600 but less than $1,000, ignoring the households’ contract cost.
More than $600 but less than $900 paid to the venue.
More than $100 but less than $400 paid to the venue.
Exactly $1,000, because the full avoided harm must become compensation.
42149.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
42149.feedback: The venue needs more than its $600 cost. Households save $1,000 but spend $100 on contracting, leaving a payment ceiling of $900. The $300 interval reflects net joint gains; payments distribute those gains.

42150.q: Why can community norms reduce an externality without guaranteeing full efficiency?
options: Norms always equate social margins
Norms eliminate all transaction costs
Coverage and enforcement may be incomplete
Voluntary action cannot affect spillovers
42150.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
42150.feedback: Private institutions can help without fully internalizing harm. Norms can change behavior, but incomplete participation and weak enforcement can leave some marginal external harm outside private decisions.

42156.q: A workshop can install a filter for $400 that avoids $900 of harm to its sole neighbor. Rights are enforceable, information is complete, bargaining is costless, and there are no wealth effects. Which prediction survives reversing the initial right to emit?
options: The filter remains worthwhile; the direction or amount of compensation can change.
The filter is worthwhile only if the neighbor initially holds the right to clean air.
The filter’s resource cost changes from $400 to $900 when rights reverse.
Both parties must receive the same income under either assignment of rights.
42156.commonError: Treating Coase bargaining as costless or as proof that initial rights never matter.
42156.feedback: The filter creates 900 - 400 = $500 in joint surplus under either rights assignment. Initial rights determine the disagreement outcome and bargaining payments, not the stated benefit-cost ranking.

42157.q: Under ideal Coase conditions, how does changing initial rights affect the result?
options: It necessarily changes efficient quantity
It can change compensation while leaving efficient allocation attainable
It affects neither efficiency nor distribution
It prevents bargaining
42157.commonError: Treating Coase bargaining as costless or as proof that initial rights never matter.
42157.feedback: Rights affect distribution even when bargaining reaches efficiency. Either rights assignment can support the efficient quantity under ideal bargaining, but it determines which party pays and how the bargaining gains are divided.

42158.q: A pollution bargain has poor information and strategic holdouts among thousands. Which Coase condition is weakest?
options: Scarcity
Downward demand
Low transaction and bargaining costs
Government tax collection
42158.commonError: Treating Coase bargaining as costless or as proof that initial rights never matter.
42158.feedback: Information, coordination, and holdouts make bargaining costly. Poor information, many participants, and strategic holdouts raise the cost of reaching and enforcing agreement, undermining the low-transaction-cost assumption.

P52B-MFAIL-L-001.q: Vaccination creates an external benefit, but a fixed number of appointments is already fully used. A subsidy is introduced without expanding capacity or changing how appointments are allocated. Which assessment best separates the externality diagnosis from this policy’s current effect?
options: Private demand rises, but vaccinations cannot rise yet; additional spillover benefits require more capacity or a better allocation.
The subsidy necessarily raises vaccinations to the efficient quantity despite the fixed appointment limit.
Fixed capacity means the external benefit disappears and the original externality diagnosis is false.
Subsidy spending itself equals new transmission benefits even when the vaccinated group is unchanged.
P52B-MFAIL-L-001.commonError: Failing to distinguish private and social benefits.
P52B-MFAIL-L-001.feedback: The external benefit can justify stronger private incentives, but supply is constrained here. With both quantity and recipients fixed, subsidizing existing appointments changes payments rather than the transmission benefit. Capacity and allocation matter for the feasible remedy.

P77-MFAIL-L-019.q: A festival can run late, end early, or run late with sound insulation. Relative to ending early, running late adds $1,000 of gains to attendees and organizers and $1,400 of resident harm. Insulation costs $600 and reduces that harm to $200. Ignore bargaining costs. Which arrangement maximizes net gains, and what remains to be negotiated?
options: End early; all late operation has negative social value even with insulation.
Run late without insulation; the $1,000 private gain establishes efficiency.
Run late with insulation; divide its $200 net gain through compensation.
Run late with insulation; resident compensation itself adds another $200 of social benefit.
P77-MFAIL-L-019.commonError: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
P77-MFAIL-L-019.feedback: Late without insulation yields 1000 - 1400 = -$400. Late with insulation yields 1000 - 600 - 200 = $200 relative to ending early. Compensation can distribute gains but is not an additional resource benefit.

P77-MFAIL-L-022.q: A health agency observes that a vaccine subsidy increases vaccinations but an unrelated change also reduces exposure to infection. Which additional evidence is needed to judge whether the subsidy improves efficiency?
options: Only the subsidy budget, because larger transfers imply larger social gains.
The marginal spillover benefit at the new quantity, the real cost of extra doses, and policy implementation costs.
Only the number of new doses, because each added dose must be efficient.
Only recipients’ private willingness to pay, because the outside benefit is already in every purchase.
P77-MFAIL-L-022.commonError: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
P77-MFAIL-L-022.feedback: A quantity increase is consistent with correcting underconsumption but does not prove optimal scale. Changed exposure can alter marginal external benefits. Evaluate incremental social benefits and real resource/implementation costs; the payment budget alone is not welfare.

42086.q: Refer to the gardens graph. Enforceable agreements could let all affected neighbors jointly pay producers $5 per garden, with no bargaining cost or wealth effects. Compare this with a $5 producer subsidy funded by costless lump-sum taxes. Which conclusion follows?
options: Both can support 150 gardens; the $750 transfer is itself the net social gain.
Only the subsidy can support 150 gardens because voluntary payments cannot change marginal incentives.
Both can support 150 gardens; who pays and receives transfers differs, while the gain over 100 gardens is $125.
Both support 100 gardens because payments do not alter the producers’ effective return.
42086.commonError: Treating Coase bargaining as costless or as proof that initial rights never matter.
42086.feedback: Either $5 payment internalizes the marginal external benefit. The gain from expanding 100 to 150 gardens is the triangle 0.5 x 50 x 5 = $125. The $750 paid on all 150 gardens redistributes purchasing power; it is not the net welfare gain.

A purple vertical bracket near Q = 150 spans the MPB-MSC value $10 to the MPC value $15.

42095.q: Refer to the transit graph. A $2 rider subsidy could implement the social-intersection quantity at a real administration cost of $12 thousand per day. A private agreement would implement the same quantity but cost $18 thousand per day to arrange and enforce. Ignore financing distortions and treat transfers as transfers. Which comparison follows?
options: The subsidy yields -$362 thousand because its entire budget is a lost social resource.
Bargaining yields $50 thousand because voluntary agreements have no real costs.
Both yield $400 thousand because payments on all rides equal the welfare gain.
The subsidy yields $38 thousand and bargaining $32 thousand in net daily gains over the private outcome.
42095.commonError: Treating Coase bargaining as costless or as proof that initial rights never matter.
42095.feedback: The graph’s gain from 150 to 200 thousand rides is 0.5 x 50 x 2 = $50 thousand per day. Subtracting real implementation costs leaves 50 - 12 = 38 and 50 - 18 = 32. This ranking depends on the stated costs, not a universal advantage of policy over bargaining.
42095.imageAlt: Graph of public-transit rides (thousands per day) with labeled marginal curves, intersection guides and a purple bracket.
42095.graphDescription: The horizontal axis measures public-transit rides (thousands per day), from 0 to 250. The vertical axis measures marginal benefit and cost in dollars per ride. MPB is a straight line from (0, $8) to (250, $3). MPC is a straight line from (0, $2) to (250, $7). MSB is a straight line from (0, $10) to (250, $5), parallel to MPB. A red dot marks the MPB-MPC intersection at (150, $5); a green dot marks the MSB-MPC intersection at (200, $6). Dashed guides project those dots to the axes. A purple vertical bracket near Q = 200 spans the MPB value $4 to the MSB-MPC value $6.

42100.q: Refer to the imperfect-correction graph. The city raises the vaping tax from $2 to the full $4 correction. Ignoring administration and financing costs, what additional welfare gain is obtained, and how does tax revenue change?
options: Welfare rises $20 thousand; revenue rises $240 thousand.
Welfare rises $240 thousand; revenue rises $20 thousand.
Welfare rises $80 thousand; revenue rises $320 thousand.
Welfare rises $40 thousand; revenue falls $240 thousand.
42100.commonError: Confusing the corrective wedge, incidence, revenue, and deadweight loss.
42100.feedback: At $2, quantity is 160 thousand and residual loss is 0.5 x (160 - 140) x 2 = $20 thousand. Full correction removes it. Revenue changes from 2 x 160 = $320 thousand to 4 x 140 = $560 thousand, an increase of $240 thousand.

A red dot marks the MPB-MPC intersection (180, $10), and a green dot marks the MSB-MPC intersection (140, $8). Dashed guides show their coordinates. A purple vertical bracket near Q = 160 spans $9 to $11 on MPB.

42103.q: Which assessment correctly compares the actual $2 vaping tax with the optimal $4 correction?
options: It restores efficiency because every positive tax is corrective
It worsens efficiency because revenue is not social surplus
It eliminates the external cost although quantity remains above 140 thousand
It improves efficiency but does not restore it because the optimal tax is $4
42103.commonError: Confusing the corrective wedge, incidence, revenue, and deadweight loss.
42103.feedback: The $2 tax reduces consumption from 180 thousand to 160 thousand, so it improves efficiency. Because MPC and MSB intersect at 140 thousand, 20 thousand vapes of overconsumption and $20 thousand of residual DWL remain.

42145.q: Two systems reach the same cap; one allocates permits equally and one auctions them. What must be separated?
options: Aggregate emissions from trading
Cost-effective emissions allocation from distribution of permit value
External cost from private cost
The cap from permit count
42145.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
42145.feedback: Allocation can change wealth without changing the least-cost emissions allocation. Both systems can reach the same least-cost allocation through trading, while the initial distribution or auction of permits changes who receives the scarcity rents.

42147.q: Plants would emit 500 tons without abatement. A binding cap is reduced to 420 tons. The first 50 tons can be abated for $10 each; the next 50 for $30 each, with no other abatement or trading costs. What allocation and total cost meet the new cap most cheaply?
options: Abate 80 low-cost tons for $800, even though only 50 are available.
Abate 40 tons in each cost group for $1,600.
Abate 420 tons because the new cap is the required reduction.
Abate all 50 low-cost tons and 30 higher-cost tons, for $1,400.
42147.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
42147.feedback: Required abatement is 500 - 420 = 80 tons. Exhaust the 50 tons at $10, then use 30 at $30: 500 + 900 = $1,400. The cap limits remaining emissions, while trading can allocate reductions to the cheaper opportunities.

42151.q: A landlord can insulate a noisy building for $700. The improvement raises the present value of rents by $500 and gives neighboring properties $400 of additional benefits. There are no other effects. Neighbors could organize a payment at a real cost of $250. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: The landlord installs without a payment because all $900 of benefits become its rent.
The proposed bargain creates $200 of net gains because coordination costs are transfers.
Insulation is socially wasteful because benefits outside the building do not count.
Insulation is socially worthwhile before coordination costs, but neither rent capture alone nor that bargain finances it with positive joint gains.
42151.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
42151.feedback: Total benefit is 500 + 400 = $900, above the $700 cost by $200. The landlord captures only $500. Coordinating neighbors consumes $250, more than the available $200 joint gain, so that arrangement does not close the incentive gap profitably.

42152.q: Thousands of dispersed residents each suffer a small pollution loss. Why may negotiation fail?
options: Organizing and bargaining costs can exceed gains
Harm becomes private benefit
Large numbers guarantee compensation
Rights cease to affect distribution
42152.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
42152.feedback: Large groups can make coordination too costly. When many parties each have small stakes, locating participants, coordinating terms, preventing holdouts, and enforcing payment can consume the bargaining surplus.

42153.q: A polluter has the right to continue operating. Option A prevents $900 of damage, costs $500 to install and $100 to contract. Option B prevents $1,200 of damage, costs $650 to install and $300 to contract. Victims pay all contract costs; transfers have no resource cost. Which option offers the larger bargaining surplus, and what payment interval supports it?
options: Option B: more than $650 but less than $900, because it prevents more damage.
Option A: more than $500 but less than $800 paid to the polluter.
Option A: more than $500 but less than $900, because contracting uses no resources.
Option B: exactly $1,200, because all avoided damage must become compensation.
42153.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
42153.feedback: A yields 900 - 500 - 100 = $300; B yields 1200 - 650 - 300 = $250. Under A, a payment above $500 covers the polluter’s cost, while one below $800 leaves victims better off after their $100 contracting cost.

42154.q: A contract creates $1,200 in joint gains but costs $350 to negotiate and enforce. What net gain remains?
42154.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
42154.feedback: Net gain is $1,200 - $350. Negotiation and enforcement costs use $350 of the $1,200 gross surplus, leaving $850 available to make the parties better off.

42155.q: Noise reduction costs $700 and benefits neighbors $1,000. Agreement costs $400. Is bargaining worthwhile?
options: Yes; every external benefit guarantees bargaining
Yes; net gain is $700
No; initial rights prevent efficiency
No; the $300 gross gain is below the $400 transaction cost
42155.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
42155.feedback: Gross gain is $300, below transaction cost. The action creates only $300 of gross joint surplus, so spending $400 to reach and enforce an agreement would make the bargain inefficient.

42159.q: Preventing a spillover avoids $2 million of harm and uses $1.2 million of resources. A bargain adds $1 million in real transaction costs. An enforceable regulation can achieve the same prevention with $0.3 million of administration and compliance costs beyond prevention. With no other effects, which ranking follows?
options: The bargain gains $0.8 million and ranks first because transfers are voluntary.
No prevention ranks first because failed bargaining proves prevention is inefficient.
Regulation loses $0.7 million because avoided harm should be excluded from policy evaluation.
Regulation gains $0.5 million; no prevention ranks next; the bargain loses $0.2 million.
42159.commonError: Treating Coase bargaining as costless or as proof that initial rights never matter.
42159.feedback: Gross prevention gains are 2 - 1.2 = $0.8 million. Net gains are 0.8 - 1 = -$0.2 million for this bargain and 0.8 - 0.3 = $0.5 million for regulation. Bargaining failure does not establish that every feasible remedy fails.

ECON-MG-EASYBOSS-2016.q: A factory pollutes a river used by nearby residents. What kind of market failure is this?
options: A negative externality
A public good
A price floor
A positive externality.
ECON-MG-EASYBOSS-2016.feedback: Pollution harms bystanders who are not part of the transaction, so it is a negative externality.

P52B-MFAIL-B2-001.q: Which case is a negative externality?
options: Noise from a venue reducing nearby residents’ well-being.
A buyer paying the posted price.
A student receiving private tutoring that affects only the student and tutor.
A firm lowering its own cost.
P52B-MFAIL-B2-001.commonError: Misidentifying the source of market failure.
P52B-MFAIL-B2-001.feedback: Noise that reduces nearby residents’ well-being imposes a cost on third parties outside the transaction, so it is a negative externality.

options: A cost or benefit affecting a third party outside the transaction.
Any change in the market price.
A government expenditure.
A cost paid fully by the buyer.
P52B-MFAIL-R-001.commonError: Calling every market effect an externality.
P52B-MFAIL-R-001.feedback: Externalities spill over to people not directly involved in the exchange.

P77-MFAIL-R-035.q: What makes an effect an externality?
options: It spills onto a third party outside the transaction
The outcome is a public good by definition
A large firm merely changes its own cost
The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
P77-MFAIL-R-035.commonError: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
P77-MFAIL-R-035.feedback: An externality affects people outside the transaction.

P77-MFAIL-BR-038.q: Pollution changes a firm’s private marginal choice. What connection matters?
options: The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
Marginal analysis can compare private and social cost
The outcome is a public good by definition
A large firm merely changes its own cost
P77-MFAIL-BR-038.commonError: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
P77-MFAIL-BR-038.feedback: Marginal analysis compares the private marginal incentives facing the firm with the social marginal cost that includes the pollution spillover.

options: Always sold by one monopoly firm
A legal maximum price
Hard to exclude people from and shared by many users
A substitute for every other good
ECON-MG-EASY-13.feedback: Public goods are generally nonexcludable and nonrival.

P77-MFAIL-E-004.q: A storm-warning signal can serve another listener without reducing its value and nonpayers are hard to exclude. What is it?
options: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
It is a private good supplied by government
A public good
It is nonrival but easy to exclude
P77-MFAIL-E-004.commonError: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
P77-MFAIL-E-004.feedback: Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude.

42180.q: Why is it too strong to claim that private firms can never participate in public-radio provision?
options: Advertising, contracts, donations, or government purchasing can create revenue
Nonexcludability guarantees subscription revenue
MC disappears for private firms
Private Benefit must always equal MSB
42180.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
42180.feedback: Alternative institutions can finance private participation even when direct listener payments understate social benefit. The underprovision result is conditional, not a claim that private participation is impossible.

42184.q: Refer to the graph. At 20 miles of coastal protection, which marginal comparison is correct?
options: MSB exceeds MC, so expanding protection raises net social benefit
MC exceeds MSB, so protection should contract
MSB equals MC, so 20 miles is efficient
Private Benefit is necessarily zero
42184.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
42184.feedback: At Q = 20, the graph shows MSB at $40 million and MC at $25 million. The next mile adds more benefit than cost.
42184.imageAlt: Coastal flood protection graph with downward-sloping MSB and upward-sloping MC intersecting at 30 miles and $30 million per mile.
42184.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is miles of coastal flood protection. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in millions of dollars per mile. MSB equals 60 minus Q and MC equals 15 plus 0.5Q. They intersect at 30 miles, where both equal $30 million per mile.

42190.q: Community-wide coastal protection can serve another resident without reducing protection for anyone else. Which characteristic does that illustrate?
options: Each protected resident removes protection from another
Only one buyer can consume each mile
Many residents receive the same protection without using it up
Open harvesting depletes the barrier
42190.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42190.feedback: Flood protection is nonrival over the stated range because protecting another resident does not subtract protection from others.

42194.q: Refer to the graph. At four displays, what marginal social benefit results from vertically summing North and South?
42194.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
42194.feedback: At Q = 4, North MB is $30,000 and South MB is $20,000. Because both consume the same display, the benefits add vertically to MSB of $50,000.
42194.imageAlt: Community fireworks graph with North MB, South MB, vertically summed MSB, and MC, with decomposition guides at four displays.
42194.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is community fireworks displays per summer. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per display. North MB is max of zero and 50 minus 5Q. South MB is max of zero and 40 minus 5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $50,000 per display. At four displays, North MB is $30,000, South MB is $20,000, and MSB equals MC at $50,000.

42200.q: Refer to the public-radio summation graph. At 40 hours, what is Group A's marginal benefit?
options: $3,000 per hour
$1,000 per hour
$2,000 per hour
$5,000 per hour
42200.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
42200.feedback: At Q = 40, the graph shows Group A's MB at 30 on an axis measured in hundreds of dollars, or $3,000 per hour.
42200.imageAlt: Public radio vertical-summation graph with Group A MB, Group B MB, MSB, and MC, highlighting 40 hours per week.
42200.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is hours of local public radio programming per week. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in hundreds of dollars per hour. Group A MB is max of zero and 50 minus 0.5Q. Group B MB is max of zero and 30 minus 0.5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $3,000 per hour. At 40 hours, Group A MB is $3,000 per hour, Group B MB is $1,000 per hour, and MSB is $4,000 per hour.

42204.q: Refer to the graph. Which calculation would misread the shared quantity at 40 hours?
options: Adding Group A's 40 hours to Group B's 40 hours to claim 80 hours
Adding marginal benefits of $3,000 and $1,000
Reporting MSB of $4,000 per hour
Recognizing both groups receive 40 hours
42204.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42204.feedback: Public-good beneficiaries share one common quantity. Their marginal benefits are added vertically; their identical consumed quantities are not added together.
42204.imageAlt: Public radio vertical-summation graph with Group A MB, Group B MB, MSB, and MC, highlighting 40 hours per week.
42204.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is hours of local public radio programming per week. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in hundreds of dollars per hour. Group A MB is max of zero and 50 minus 0.5Q. Group B MB is max of zero and 30 minus 0.5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $3,000 per hour. At 40 hours, Group A MB is $3,000 per hour, Group B MB is $1,000 per hour, and MSB is $4,000 per hour.

42211.q: A winter coat is sold to one customer and cannot be worn by another customer at the same time. What category fits?
options: Public good
Common resource
Club good
Private good
42211.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42211.feedback: The seller can exclude nonbuyers, and one person's use prevents simultaneous use by another, so the coat is excludable and rival.

42215.q: A university database requires a paid login, and simultaneous users do not reduce the information available to one another. Which category fits?
options: Public good
Private good
Common resource
Club good
42215.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42215.feedback: The login permits exclusion of nonmembers, while digital access is nonrival under the stated capacity conditions.

42221.q: Anyone may fish in a lake, but each catch leaves fewer fish for other anglers. How should the fishery be classified?
options: Public good
Common resource
Private good
Club good
42221.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42221.feedback: Open access makes exclusion difficult, while catches deplete the stock available to others, so the resource is nonexcludable and rival.

42225.q: A research archive places its digital articles behind a paywall, and additional readers do not reduce access quality. What category applies?
options: Public good
Club good
Private good
Common resource
42225.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42225.feedback: The paywall makes the archive excludable, while digital reading is nonrival over the stated capacity range.

42232.q: A lake has no fences, permits, or patrols. Which fact most directly supports nonexcludability?
options: Preventing unapproved users from reaching the lake is impractical
Fish are scarce
Anglers compete in tournaments
The lake has measurable depth
42232.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
42232.feedback: Nonexcludability concerns the feasibility of denying access, not whether the resource is scarce or whether users compete.

42236.q: A toll transponder is required to enter a bridge. What is the direct economic effect of the transponder system?
options: It creates a practical way to exclude nonpayers
It guarantees the bridge is uncongested
It makes each crossing nonrival
It eliminates maintenance costs
42236.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
42236.feedback: The transponder controls access and makes exclusion feasible. Congestion determines rivalry separately.

42243.q: One commuter occupies the last seat on a bus. What does this show?
options: The seat is nonrival because the bus follows a route
The seat is excludable only if government owns it
The seat reflects rivalry among bus companies
The seat is rival because it is unavailable to another commuter
42243.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
42243.feedback: A seat used by one passenger cannot simultaneously serve another, so consumption of that seat is rival.

42247.q: Why is groundwater rival in consumption?
options: Groundwater users compete in product markets
The aquifer can never be fenced
Water has a positive price
Water pumped by one user reduces the stock available to others
42247.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
42247.feedback: Rivalry follows from depletion: one user's withdrawal leaves less groundwater for other users.

42254.q: A household understates how much it values flood protection during a voluntary fundraising survey. What motive may explain the response?
options: It wants the barrier to become rival
It cannot benefit if another household pays
It hopes to lower its payment while still receiving protection
It is revealing the full social benefit
42254.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
42254.feedback: Because protection reaches the household even if it contributes little, understating willingness to pay can reduce its expected share of the cost.

42258.q: Which statement best distinguishes a free rider from someone who receives no benefit?
options: A free rider pays but cannot consume
A free rider depletes an open-access resource
A free rider benefits but does not pay or contribute
A free rider always breaks a law
42258.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
42258.feedback: Free riding requires receiving a benefit without contributing toward its cost; a person who receives no benefit is not riding on others' provision.

42264.q: Why can a unanimous claim that 'someone else will fund it' be self-defeating for a public good?
options: If everyone withholds payment, a valued project may not be provided
Withholding makes MSB equal zero
The project becomes rival
The project is necessarily overprovided
42264.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
42264.feedback: Individually attractive free riding can produce a collective outcome in which contributions are too small to finance a project whose total social benefit exceeds cost.

42269.q: Which statement about private firms and public goods is economically accurate?
options: Private firms never provide anything nonrival
Private firms can participate when contracts, advertising, donations, or public purchasing create revenue
Profit requires every good to be rival
Government ownership is part of the definition of a public good
42269.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
42269.feedback: The underprovision result is conditional, not absolute. Alternative revenue arrangements can support private production even when direct exclusion of beneficiaries is difficult.

42275.q: A charitable foundation pays for open scientific data. Which conclusion is best?
options: The data become rival because a foundation paid
The data are a private good because funding is private
Free riding is impossible whenever donors exist
A private organization can finance a public good without charging each user
42275.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
42275.feedback: Foundation funding is an alternative financing mechanism. The open data can remain nonexcludable and nonrival even though a private organization pays for them.

42280.q: Which challenge arises when benefits from flood protection occur decades in the future?
options: Future and uncertain benefits must be estimated and compared with current costs
Future benefits are automatically zero
Marginal cost stops mattering
The project becomes a private good
42280.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
42280.feedback: Long horizons require forecasts and comparison of benefits and costs occurring at different times, adding uncertainty to valuation.

42286.q: Farmers pumping from a shared aquifer ignore how their withdrawals raise future pumping costs for neighbors. What is the likely outcome?
options: Groundwater is underprovided like a public good
The aquifer becomes nonrival
Groundwater is withdrawn faster than is socially efficient
Every farmer automatically conserves the efficient amount
42286.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42286.feedback: Each farmer captures the crop benefit while sharing depletion and pumping-cost effects with others, encouraging aggregate withdrawal above the efficient level.

42290.q: A forest is open to unrestricted fuelwood harvesting. Which pattern signals tragedy-of-the-commons pressure?
options: Households pay owners for every tree
New trees are nonrival
Each household harvests without accounting for reduced timber available to others
A single owner bears the full future loss
42290.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42290.feedback: Open access and rival harvesting let households capture fuelwood benefits while shifting part of the stock loss to other users.

42294.q: A city adds road capacity and congestion briefly falls, but free access attracts more trips. Which risk remains?
options: Capacity makes road space permanently nonrival
Drivers become excludable without a toll
Untolled access can again produce excessive use at congested times
The road becomes a pure public good at every quantity
42294.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42294.feedback: Additional capacity can delay congestion, but when use is free at the margin drivers still omit delay imposed on others and overuse can return.

42296.q: What would an efficient common-resource rule try to make users consider?
options: The opportunity cost their use imposes on other users
Only their private benefit
Only historical average cost
Whether the resource is publicly named
42296.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42296.feedback: Efficiency requires users to compare private benefit with the full social opportunity cost, including depletion or congestion imposed on others.

42298.q: Why might voluntary promises alone fail to protect a large open-access forest?
options: The forest is nonrival
Promises automatically create enforceable ownership
Each user can gain by harvesting while relying on others to restrain themselves
Conservation has no social benefit
42298.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42298.feedback: Without monitoring or enforceable access rules, an individual can privately benefit from violating restraint while the stock cost is dispersed.

42300.q: Which policy logic directly addresses common-resource overuse?
options: Limit or price access so users face more of the depletion or congestion cost
Subsidize every additional unit of use
Make the resource less excludable
Ignore aggregate use and track only private benefit
42300.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42300.feedback: Access limits, user charges, or enforceable rights connect individual choices more closely to the social cost of using a rival shared resource.

42302.q: Why can common-resource use exceed the efficient quantity even when every user understands depletion?
options: Information automatically removes the incentive
Understanding makes the resource nonrival
Each user may still capture a private gain while bearing only part of the shared cost
Efficiency requires zero resource use
42302.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42302.feedback: Knowledge alone does not align incentives. A user's private gain can exceed the personal share of depletion cost even when the full social cost is larger.

42305.q: What is required for a legal property right to change resource-use incentives?
options: The resource must become nonrival
The right must be sufficiently clear and enforceable
All transaction costs must be zero
Every user must value the resource equally
42305.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
42305.feedback: Users respond to rights when boundaries and permissions are clear and violations can be detected and sanctioned.

42307.q: Why might a private forest owner conserve young trees?
options: Ownership makes harvesting nonrival
The owner cannot exclude trespassers
Conservation always has zero current cost
Future timber value is part of the owner's private opportunity cost of harvesting now
42307.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
42307.feedback: Secure ownership lets the owner capture future forest value, so cutting a young tree carries a private cost that open-access harvesters may ignore.

42308.q: A toll is introduced on a congested road. How can this improve resource-use incentives?
options: Drivers face a price connected to scarce road capacity and delay
The toll makes road space unlimited
The toll guarantees no congestion at any price
Drivers stop receiving private trip benefits
42308.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
42308.feedback: A toll can make access excludable and require drivers to consider more of the congestion cost associated with scarce road space.

42309.q: Which claim about assigning property rights is too strong?
options: Enforcement matters
Property rights automatically produce perfect efficiency in every setting
Monitoring can be costly
Rights can improve conservation incentives
42309.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
42309.feedback: Rights can align incentives, but unclear boundaries, weak enforcement, ecological spillovers, market power, and transaction costs can prevent a perfect outcome.

42310.q: An exclusive grazing lease is never monitored, and outsiders continue using the land. What is the main problem?
options: Grazing has become nonrival
The lease creates free riding on a public good
The right is not effectively enforceable
Ownership eliminates the need for boundaries
42310.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
42310.feedback: A paper lease does not create practical exclusion when unauthorized grazing cannot be detected or stopped.

Fishers no longer need to capture their allowed share before everyone else

The holder can benefit from preserving future availability
The right removes all uncertainty

Property rights require a market price of zero
Migration eliminates social value
The resource crosses boundaries and is costly to monitor

The fish stock has become nonrival
Outsider exclusion is the only relevant incentive
The cooperative has created a public good
42316.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.

42317.q: How do clear rights differ from a general request to conserve?

Clear rights specify who may use the resource and who bears gains or losses from stewardship
Clear rights eliminate marginal cost
A request guarantees penalties for overuse
42317.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
42317.feedback: Defined rights connect authorized use and future resource value to identifiable decision-makers, while a general request may leave access and consequences diffuse.

42318.q: Which combination is most likely to reduce open-access overuse?

More users with identical extraction incentives
Clear access rights, feasible monitoring, and credible enforcement
A rule that cannot detect violations
42318.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
42318.feedback: Rights alter behavior most reliably when users know the boundaries, compliance can be observed, and violations carry credible consequences.

42219.q: A citywide mosquito-control program benefits properties throughout the treated area, including nonpayers, without reducing protection for others. Which category fits?

Club good
Public good

Common resource
Club good

42224.q: A downtown road has no toll and is heavily congested. What category best describes road space at that time?

Club good
