42279.q: How can free riding bias a survey used to value a proposed public good?
options: Respondents must overstate marginal cost
The survey makes the good rival
Only nonbeneficiaries answer surveys
Respondents may understate willingness to pay if answers affect their expected contribution
42279.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
42279.feedback: People who expect to receive the good regardless of payment may report low values to reduce their expected cost share.

42281.q: Why might voluntary donations be a poor measure of total benefit from a public warning system?
options: Donations include only marginal cost
Noncontributors can benefit, so donations omit part of willingness to pay
Warning systems are rival
Total benefit equals government spending
42281.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
42281.feedback: Observed gifts reflect contributed private payments, not necessarily the full value received by contributors and free riders.

42284.q: Why do boats tend to catch too many fish in an open-access fishery?
options: Each boat receives the catch benefit but shares the depletion cost with all users
Fish are nonrival
Each boat pays the full opportunity cost imposed on others
Open access guarantees conservation
42284.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42284.feedback: A boat captures much of its private gain while imposing part of the reduced future stock on other boats, so private incentives favor excessive harvest.

42287.q: On open grazing land, why might each herder add another animal even when total grazing is excessive?
options: Forage is nonrival
The herder bears every depletion cost
Adding animals makes the land excludable
The herder gets the added animal's benefit while spreading pasture damage across all herders
42287.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42287.feedback: Private benefit is concentrated, while reduced forage and land damage are shared, so individual incentives can produce collective overgrazing.

42289.q: Why is the tragedy of the commons an incentive problem rather than merely selfish behavior?
options: Common resources have no value
Open access separates private gains from part of the social depletion cost
All users prefer destroying the resource
Rivalry eliminates scarcity
42289.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42289.feedback: Even ordinary users face an incentive to take the private benefit now because much of the depletion cost falls on the group.

42291.q: Which outcome distinguishes common-resource overuse from public-good underprovision?
options: Both necessarily have insufficient use
Both are excludable and rival
Public goods are depleted while common resources are not
Common resources tend toward excessive use, while public goods tend toward insufficient provision
42291.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42291.feedback: Nonexcludable public goods invite free riding on payment and underprovision; rival common resources invite use without full depletion cost and overuse.

42293.q: Why can an individual fisher's private marginal cost be below the social marginal cost of a catch?
options: Fish are a public good
The fisher does not bear the full reduction in future catch opportunities for others
The fisher pays every stock cost immediately
Social cost excludes depletion
42293.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42293.feedback: The private calculation omits part of the opportunity cost imposed on other users through a smaller future stock.

P52B-MFAIL-H-002.q: Why can a common resource be overused?
options: It is nonrival and nonexcludable.
Users receive the private benefit while sharing depletion costs with others.
Its price is always above marginal cost.
No one can access it.
P52B-MFAIL-H-002.commonError: Confusing common resources with public goods.
P52B-MFAIL-H-002.feedback: Common resources are rival but difficult to exclude, creating overuse incentives.

P77-MFAIL-H-012.q: A lake is rival in use but access is difficult to restrict. Which problem fits?
options: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
It is a private good supplied by government
A common-resource overuse problem
It is nonrival but easy to exclude
P77-MFAIL-H-012.commonError: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
P77-MFAIL-H-012.feedback: Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude.

42182.q: Refer to the coastal-protection graph. A council has funds for either 20, 30 or 40 miles and wants the greatest net social benefit. Which choice is supported by marginal benefit and cost?
options: 40 miles: the longest affordable barrier must maximize net social benefit.
20 miles: lower marginal cost makes every shorter barrier more efficient.
30 miles: expand beyond 20 while MSB exceeds MC, but do not add the miles beyond 30.
Either 20 or 40 miles: equal distances from the intersection imply equal maximum benefit.
42182.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
42182.feedback: The graph has MSB above MC below 30 miles and below MC above 30. Expanding to their intersection adds worthwhile protection; further expansion costs more than its added benefit. Affordability alone is not the efficiency rule.
42182.imageAlt: Coastal flood protection graph with downward-sloping MSB and upward-sloping MC intersecting at 30 miles and $30 million per mile.
42182.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is miles of coastal flood protection. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in millions of dollars per mile. MSB equals 60 minus Q and MC equals 15 plus 0.5Q. They intersect at 30 miles, where both equal $30 million per mile.

42187.q: Suppose a coastal barrier protects all shoreline residents, nonpayers cannot be excluded, and protecting another household does not reduce anyone else's protection. How is it classified?
options: Private good
Common resource
Club good
Public good
42187.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42187.feedback: The barrier is nonexcludable because shoreline nonpayers still receive protection and nonrival because protecting another household does not reduce protection for others.

42192.q: Refer to the fireworks graph. At four shared displays, an analyst records only North’s marginal benefit and recommends reducing provision because it is below MC. What corrects this recommendation?
options: Add South’s $20,000 to North’s $30,000; the fourth shared display meets the $50,000 marginal cost.
Add the neighborhoods’ quantities to obtain eight displays and compare that with MC.
Use only North’s $30,000 because the larger valuation replaces the smaller one.
Average the two valuations to obtain $25,000 and reduce provision.
42192.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
42192.feedback: Both neighborhoods consume the same four displays. The marginal values add vertically: 30,000 + 20,000 = $50,000, equal to MC. Neither a quantity sum nor an average values the shared marginal display correctly.
42192.imageAlt: Community fireworks graph with North MB, South MB, vertically summed MSB, and MC, with decomposition guides at four displays.
42192.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is community fireworks displays per summer. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per display. North MB is max of zero and 50 minus 5Q. South MB is max of zero and 40 minus 5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $50,000 per display. At four displays, North MB is $30,000, South MB is $20,000, and MSB equals MC at $50,000.

42197.q: The graph plots North and South MB at the same quantity of four displays. Which summation rule does this illustrate?
options: Public-good quantities are summed at a common price
Public-good marginal benefits are summed at a common quantity
Public-good marginal cost is always zero
Private-good buyers must consume identical quantities
42197.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42197.feedback: For a shared public good, everyone receives the same quantity, so marginal willingness to pay is added vertically. Private-good market demand usually sums individual quantities horizontally at a price.
42197.imageAlt: Community fireworks graph with North MB, South MB, vertically summed MSB, and MC, with decomposition guides at four displays.
42197.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is community fireworks displays per summer. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per display. North MB is max of zero and 50 minus 5Q. South MB is max of zero and 40 minus 5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $50,000 per display. At four displays, North MB is $30,000, South MB is $20,000, and MSB equals MC at $50,000.

42202.q: Refer to the graph. What is MSB at 40 hours after vertically summing the two groups' marginal benefits?
options: $1,000 per hour
$2,000 per hour
$4,000 per hour
$6,000 per hour
42202.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
42202.feedback: At Q = 40, Group A MB is $3,000 and Group B MB is $1,000. Their vertical sum gives MSB of $4,000 per hour.
42202.imageAlt: Public radio vertical-summation graph with Group A MB, Group B MB, MSB, and MC, highlighting 40 hours per week.
42202.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is hours of local public radio programming per week. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in hundreds of dollars per hour. Group A MB is max of zero and 50 minus 0.5Q. Group B MB is max of zero and 30 minus 0.5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $3,000 per hour. At 40 hours, Group A MB is $3,000 per hour, Group B MB is $1,000 per hour, and MSB is $4,000 per hour.

42207.q: The graph vertically sums Group A and Group B MB at the same 40 hours. Which description best fits the represented programming?
options: A rival private good divided between two buyers
An open-access resource depleted by listening
A service whose marginal cost equals each individual's MB
A shared nonrival service whose beneficiaries have different willingness to pay
42207.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42207.feedback: Vertical summation applies because both groups consume the same nonrival programming while assigning different marginal values to it.
42207.imageAlt: Public radio vertical-summation graph with Group A MB, Group B MB, MSB, and MC, highlighting 40 hours per week.
42207.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is hours of local public radio programming per week. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in hundreds of dollars per hour. Group A MB is max of zero and 50 minus 0.5Q. Group B MB is max of zero and 30 minus 0.5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $3,000 per hour. At 40 hours, Group A MB is $3,000 per hour, Group B MB is $1,000 per hour, and MSB is $4,000 per hour.

42213.q: A gallon of gasoline is available only to a paying buyer and is gone after that buyer burns it. Which classification applies?
options: Public good
Private good
Common resource
Club good
42213.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42213.feedback: Payment makes gasoline excludable and burning a gallon prevents anyone else from consuming that gallon, so it is rival.

42218.q: A missile-defense shield protects residents whether or not they contribute, and protecting one resident does not reduce protection for others. What is it?
options: Private good
Common resource
Public good
Club good
42218.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42218.feedback: Noncontributors are difficult to exclude and protection is nonrival, so the shield has the defining characteristics of a public good.

42223.q: Herders may graze animals on unfenced public land, and added grazing leaves less forage for other herds. What is the land's use category?
options: Public good
Private good
Club good
Common resource
42223.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42223.feedback: The open land is difficult to exclude, while forage is rival because one herd's consumption reduces what remains.

42229.q: A theater can check tickets at the door. What makes a performance excludable?
options: One audience member enjoys the performance
People without valid tickets can be denied entry
Several theaters compete for customers
The performance has a cultural benefit
42229.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
42229.feedback: Excludability asks whether access can feasibly be denied. Ticket inspection lets the theater prevent nonpayers from entering.

42234.q: Why does legal ownership not by itself guarantee excludability for offshore fish stocks?
options: Ownership makes fish nonrival
Legal rights eliminate migration
The boundary must also be monitored and enforced
Excludability depends only on market price
42234.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
42234.feedback: A right changes access only when violations can be detected and prevented. Mobile fish and costly monitoring can limit practical exclusion.

42239.q: An apartment building's rooftop is accessible only with a resident key. What does the key establish?
options: Nonrivalry at every crowding level
A lack of scarcity
Competition among landlords
Excludability
42239.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
42239.feedback: The key lets the building deny access to nonresidents. Whether resident use is rival depends on capacity and congestion.

42245.q: A swimming pool is nearly empty in the morning but packed in the afternoon. Which conclusion is best?
options: The pool is rival only when membership fees rise
Rivalry can emerge when congestion reduces swimming space
Excludability disappears when crowded
Its classification can never change during the day
42245.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
42245.feedback: With spare capacity, another swimmer may impose little cost. When crowded, added use reduces space and quality for others, making use rival.

42250.q: A public lecture is livestreamed with unlimited server capacity. Which use is nonrival?
options: Occupying the final seat in the hall
Taking the only printed handout
Watching the stream
Using the speaker's time for a private meeting
42250.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
42250.feedback: Another online viewer does not reduce the stream available to others, unlike scarce seats, handouts, or private time.

42256.q: A shared warning service costs $600 and will be provided only if fully funded. Four households each value it at $200; nonpayers cannot be excluded. Three have irrevocably contributed $150 each. What is the fourth household’s best choice if it cares only about its own net benefit?
options: Contribute the remaining $150: its contribution is pivotal and leaves a $50 net benefit.
Contribute nothing: a nonpayer can enjoy the service even if it is never funded.
Contribute $200: full willingness to pay is the minimum needed to finish funding.
Contribute nothing: total social benefit below $600 makes the service inefficient.
42256.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
42256.feedback: The shortfall is 600 - 3 x 150 = $150. Without that payment the service is not provided; paying leaves 200 - 150 = $50. Nonexcludability creates free-riding incentives, but a pivotal contribution can still be privately worthwhile.

42261.q: A city asks households to report benefits from a proposed siren network before setting voluntary fees. What bias should analysts anticipate?
options: Households must overstate benefits because sirens are rival
Households may understate benefits to avoid paying
Reported benefits automatically equal MSB
Only businesses can free ride
42261.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
42261.feedback: A household may hope others finance the network while it still receives warnings, so stated willingness to pay can be biased downward.

42266.q: A voluntary radio drive raises enough for 30 hours even though listeners collectively value 50 hours above cost. What explains the gap?
options: The radio hours are depleted by listening
Marginal social benefit must be below private benefit
Private contributions omit some benefits enjoyed by noncontributors
The fundraiser makes the signal excludable
42266.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
42266.feedback: Free riding causes revealed private contributions to fall short of total social willingness to pay, so funded programming can remain below the efficient amount.

42272.q: Why might a donation-funded flood barrier be smaller than the efficient barrier?
options: Individual donations may not capture benefits received by noncontributors
Flood protection is consumed by one donor at a time
Donations make marginal cost negative
Efficient provision ignores social benefits
42272.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
42272.feedback: Noncontributors still receive protection, so voluntary revenue can understate total social willingness to pay and finance too little protection.

42278.q: Why is cost-benefit analysis difficult when a public good has no ordinary market price?
options: Public goods have no opportunity cost
Marginal benefit cannot be positive
Analysts lack a direct price signal revealing beneficiaries' willingness to pay
Market prices always overstate social value
42278.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
42278.feedback: Without ordinary purchases and prices, analysts must estimate benefits that market transactions do not directly reveal.

42283.q: Which statement best compares efficient provision of a public good with an ordinary private good?
options: Public goods ignore marginal cost
Private goods require vertical summation of all buyers at one quantity
Public goods are efficient whenever government supplies them
Both use marginal benefit versus marginal cost, but public-good benefit is harder to observe and aggregate
42283.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
42283.feedback: The same marginal efficiency principle applies, but nonexcludability, free riding, dispersed benefits, and missing market prices make public-good MSB harder to estimate.

42288.q: An extra trip on a free congested road gives its driver $12 of benefit and $8 of private time and fuel cost. It also adds $6 of delays to other drivers. Which marginal comparison explains excessive use?
options: The driver gains $4 privately, but the trip reduces net social benefit by $2.
The driver gains $4 and society gains the same $4 because the road is free.
The driver loses $2 privately because all delays to others are already in private cost.
Society gains $10 because other drivers’ delay should be added to the trip’s benefit.
42288.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42288.feedback: Private net benefit is 12 - 8 = $4. Social net benefit is 12 - 8 - 6 = -$2. The omitted congestion cost can make an individually attractive trip socially undesirable.

42292.q: A coastal shellfish bed is open to everyone. Harvesters rush to collect shellfish before others do. What dynamic is present?
options: A race to capture a rival stock before competitors deplete it
Vertical summation of public-good demand
Private underprovision caused by nonrivalry
Exclusion through property rights
42292.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42292.feedback: Open access and rivalry create a race to extract because shellfish left in the bed may be taken by another harvester.

42295.q: A shared irrigation canal has ample water this month, but supply is scarce during drought. Which statement is best?
options: The canal is always nonrival because it is shared
Drought automatically creates excludability
Government ownership eliminates depletion
Rivalry can become important when withdrawals reduce water available to others
42295.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42295.feedback: When water is scarce, one user's withdrawal directly reduces availability for others, strengthening common-resource incentives.

42297.q: An open-access fishery is biologically sustainable at 1,000 tons, but total intended catch is 1,400 tons. What problem is indicated?
options: The fishery is underprovided by 400 tons
Planned harvest exceeds the sustainable shared-resource limit
Fish consumption is nonrival
Private firms cannot harvest fish
42297.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42297.feedback: Total intended catch exceeds the sustainable amount by 400 tons, consistent with open-access incentives for excessive harvest.

42299.q: A lake's water quality falls as unrestricted boat traffic rises. Which fact is necessary for a common-resource diagnosis?
options: A government agency owns the lake
Boat makers compete
Some visitors dislike boating
Additional use reduces the quality available to other users
42299.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42299.feedback: The diagnosis requires rival use: added traffic must diminish water quality or enjoyment available to others while access remains difficult to exclude.

42301.q: A fishery announces a total catch limit, but fishers can hide landings at unmonitored docks. Which complementary change most directly addresses the reason actual harvest can exceed the announced limit?
options: Allocate paper quotas equally while leaving all landings unobserved.
Measure landings across docks and enforce catch rights against unreported harvest.
Let quota holders trade on paper while leaving hidden catches unpenalized.
Pay a subsidy per landed fish while keeping detection unchanged.
42301.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42301.feedback: A limit constrains actual use only if catches are measured and violations matter. Equal allocations and trading can affect distribution or compliance cost, but neither resolves this stated monitoring gap by itself.

42304.q: How can enforceable fishing rights reduce overharvesting?
options: Right holders bear more of the loss from depleting the future stock
Rights make fish nonrival
Rights eliminate every monitoring cost
Rights guarantee equal income for fishers
42304.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
42304.feedback: A secure claim to future harvest gives the holder a reason to preserve stock value rather than race to take fish before others do.

42306.q: A village assigns each household a monitored groundwater allowance. What incentive changes?
options: Groundwater becomes nonrival
Future scarcity disappears
Households face a clearer limit on the opportunity cost of withdrawal
Every household must pump its full allowance
42306.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
42306.feedback: A monitored allowance replaces unrestricted access with enforceable use rights, reducing the incentive to pump before others do.

42166.q: Refer to the graph. A proposal would reduce siren provision from 40 to 35. What is the economic effect at the margin?
options: It removes sirens whose marginal cost exceeds marginal social benefit
It leaves the efficient quantity unchanged
It removes sirens whose marginal social benefit exceeds marginal cost
It makes the siren system rival in consumption
42166.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
42166.feedback: Below the 40-siren intersection, the graph places MSB above MC. Cutting provision to 35 sacrifices units whose added social benefit exceeds their cost.
42166.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.
42166.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

42176.q: Why would adding programming beyond 40 hours raise net social benefit in this graph?
options: MSB remains above MC until 80 hours
Private Benefit remains above MC until 80 hours
MC is zero after 40 hours
The good becomes excludable after 40 hours
42176.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
42176.feedback: Between 40 and 80 hours, Private Benefit is below MC but MSB is above MC. Private incentives stop too soon even though additional programming still creates net social gains.
42176.imageAlt: Local public radio graph: Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours and MSB intersects MC at 80 hours per week.
42176.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is hours of local public radio programming per week. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in hundreds of dollars per hour. MSB equals 100 minus Q, Private Benefit equals 60 minus Q, and MC equals 20. Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours; MSB intersects MC at 80 hours.

42186.q: Refer to the coastal-protection graph. A cost-saving method lowers MC by $15 million per mile at every quantity, with MSB unchanged. Treat quantity as continuous. Which revised target and reasoning are consistent with the graph?
options: 30 miles, because the old intersection remains efficient whenever benefits are unchanged.
60 miles, because zero MSB is the efficient stopping condition after costs fall.
40 miles, where MSB of $20 million equals the new MC of $20 million per mile.
20 miles, because lower cost requires a lower provision target.
42186.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
42186.feedback: The original curves are MSB = 60 - Q and MC = 15 + 0.5Q in millions per mile. New MC = 0.5Q. Equating 60 - Q with 0.5Q gives Q = 40 and both margins equal 20.
42186.imageAlt: Coastal flood protection graph with downward-sloping MSB and upward-sloping MC intersecting at 30 miles and $30 million per mile.
42186.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is miles of coastal flood protection. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in millions of dollars per mile. MSB equals 60 minus Q and MC equals 15 plus 0.5Q. They intersect at 30 miles, where both equal $30 million per mile.

42196.q: Refer to the fireworks graph. Suppose an analyst finds a previously omitted neighborhood with constant marginal benefit of $10,000 per display over the relevant range. MC and the two plotted neighborhood values are unchanged. Using the continuous quantity approximation, what target follows?
options: 5 displays; the added neighborhood raises MSB to $50,000 at that quantity.
4 displays; adding beneficiaries cannot change a nonrival good’s efficient quantity.
6 displays; the omitted $10,000 is added horizontally to the original quantity.
3 displays; sharing the display among more neighborhoods lowers summed benefit.
42196.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
42196.feedback: Between four and five displays both plotted neighborhood benefits remain positive. Their sum is 90 - 10Q in thousands; including the omitted 10 gives 100 - 10Q. Setting this equal to MC = 50 gives five displays.
42196.imageAlt: Community fireworks graph with North MB, South MB, vertically summed MSB, and MC, with decomposition guides at four displays.
42196.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is community fireworks displays per summer. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per display. North MB is max of zero and 50 minus 5Q. South MB is max of zero and 40 minus 5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $50,000 per display. At four displays, North MB is $30,000, South MB is $20,000, and MSB equals MC at $50,000.

42206.q: Refer to the graph. What does Group B's $1,000 MB at 40 hours show about using Group A alone to value the broadcast?
options: It would double-count marginal cost
It would prove the signal is rival
It would omit part of the social willingness to pay
It would make Group B's quantity zero
42206.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
42206.feedback: Group B values the same marginal hour at $1,000. Ignoring that benefit understates MSB and can weaken the funding signal.
42206.imageAlt: Public radio vertical-summation graph with Group A MB, Group B MB, MSB, and MC, highlighting 40 hours per week.
42206.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is hours of local public radio programming per week. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in hundreds of dollars per hour. Group A MB is max of zero and 50 minus 0.5Q. Group B MB is max of zero and 30 minus 0.5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $3,000 per hour. At 40 hours, Group A MB is $3,000 per hour, Group B MB is $1,000 per hour, and MSB is $4,000 per hour.

42217.q: A members-only pool is uncrowded most mornings but congested on weekend afternoons. Management can sell additional unlimited memberships or require reservations only at crowded times. Which assessment uses both goods characteristics?
options: Membership makes consumption nonrival at every time, so reservations cannot address an economic constraint.
Access remains excludable; timed reservations can address peak rivalry without limiting uncrowded use.
Afternoon crowding removes the ability to exclude nonmembers, so the pool becomes open access.
Private ownership makes both morning and afternoon use rival regardless of crowding.
42217.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42217.feedback: The gate controls exclusion throughout the day. Congestion changes whether another swimmer reduces others’ enjoyment. Reservations targeted to crowded periods address that scarcity while preserving nonrival opportunities when capacity is ample.

42227.q: A road is free and uncongested before rush hour but becomes crowded later. Which conclusion is best?
options: It must be a private good at every hour
Government ownership makes it permanently public
A road can never be rival
Its classification can shift as congestion changes rivalry
42227.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42227.feedback: The road may be nonrival when uncongested and rival when crowded. Goods are classified from actual access and consumption conditions, not a permanent label.

42238.q: Which change would most directly make a previously open campground excludable?
options: Adding more campsites
Publishing a map
A staffed gate that checks reservations
Reducing competition among nearby campgrounds
42238.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
42238.feedback: A staffed gate can deny entry to people without reservations, directly changing the feasibility of exclusion.

42249.q: A cooperative excludes outsiders from a forest, but members may harvest without individual limits. Trees take years to regrow, and extra cutting now reduces future timber. Which proposed inference is justified?
options: Once outsiders are excluded, timber becomes nonrival among the remaining members.
External exclusion alone does not resolve rivalry among members; internal harvest rules can still be valuable.
Regrowth means a tree harvested now leaves the same future quantity available to others.
Cooperative ownership removes each member’s incentive to take timber before another member does.
42249.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
42249.feedback: Harvesting removes a rival stock and sacrifices future availability. Exclusion of outsiders defines a group boundary, but without internal rules the members can still race to extract. Neither regrowth nor ownership by itself eliminates the opportunity cost.

42260.q: Why does free riding not imply that nobody will ever contribute?
options: Some people may donate, but each still has an incentive to rely on others
The good becomes excludable after one donation
Rivalry guarantees full financing
Marginal cost becomes zero
42260.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
42260.feedback: Altruism, norms, or selective benefits can support contributions. The economic point is that nonexcludability weakens the payment incentive and can create underprovision.

42271.q: A county hires a private contractor to operate emergency sirens. Does private operation make the warning a private good?
options: Yes; any privately produced service is a private good
Yes; contracts make warnings rival
No; all government purchases are common resources
No; classification still depends on excludability and rivalry
42271.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
42271.feedback: Who produces or purchases the service is separate from its consumption characteristics. An area-wide warning can remain nonexcludable and nonrival.

42282.q: An analyst values a public-health information campaign using only benefits to people who completed a survey. What may be missing?
options: The campaign's excludability must be zero
Every unobserved benefit is a cost
Benefits to affected people who were not identified or surveyed
Only the producer's profit matters
42282.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
42282.feedback: Public-good benefits can be dispersed, so failing to identify all affected beneficiaries understates marginal social benefit.

P52B-MFAIL-L-002.q: A fishery is open to many boats, and each boat ignores how its catch reduces future stocks for others. Which policy logic fits?
options: Subsidize every additional catch.
Limit or price access so users face more of the depletion cost.
Remove all information about stocks.
Set a price ceiling on fish without limiting harvest.
P52B-MFAIL-L-002.commonError: Choosing a policy that strengthens overuse incentives.
P52B-MFAIL-L-002.feedback: Access rules, quotas, or charges can internalize the shared depletion cost.

P77-MFAIL-L-016.q: A navigation app is nonrival after creation but can exclude unpaid users. What is the best conclusion?
options: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
It is a private good supplied by government
It is nonrival but easy to exclude
It is not a pure public good because exclusion is feasible
P77-MFAIL-L-016.commonError: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
P77-MFAIL-L-016.feedback: The app is nonrival but excludable, so it is not a pure public good; it is closer to a club good.

P77-MFAIL-L-017.q: A fishery uses quotas, but regulators cannot observe illegal catch. What complicates the remedy?
options: Enforcement and information constraints affect performance
Any intervention is automatically costless
Identifying failure proves one remedy is optimal
Administrative incentives and information do not matter
P77-MFAIL-L-017.commonError: Treating identified failure as proof that any intervention is superior.
P77-MFAIL-L-017.feedback: Compare feasible responses, administrative costs, information limits, and unintended effects.

P77-MFAIL-L-023.q: An open-access aquifer is depleted. What private-social divergence occurs?
options: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
It is rival with fully enforceable private access
Each user ignores depletion costs shared by others
It is a private good supplied by government
P77-MFAIL-L-023.commonError: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
P77-MFAIL-L-023.feedback: Each user receives the private benefit of pumping water but bears only part of the depletion cost imposed on other users, creating an incentive to overuse the aquifer.

42210.q: A town hires contractors to supply rival packed meals, an uncrowded archive behind a login, and an unencrypted nonrival warning broadcast. It proposes charging for each meal, opening the archive after securing full sponsorship, and coordinating payment for the warning through a binding community agreement. Which assessment links the goods characteristics to those funding choices?
options: Private contractors make all three goods rival, so each additional user must be rationed through an individual charge.
Opening the archive turns it into a depleted common resource, while collecting warning contributions makes warning reception excludable.
Meals still require allocation among rival users; sponsorship can finance open nonrival access; the agreement can address warning-service free riding.
Meal fees solve the warning’s free-rider problem automatically, so the community agreement cannot change provision.
42210.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42210.feedback: Meal consumption uses up a rival unit. Archive exclusion can change without creating rivalry, and sponsorship can replace login revenue. The warning remains nonexcludable, but a binding funding agreement can coordinate contributions. Consumption characteristics and financing institutions must be evaluated separately.

42220.q: A freely broadcast emergency alert reaches every receiver in range and one listener does not weaken the signal for another. What is it?
options: Public good
Private good
Common resource
Club good
42220.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42220.feedback: The open signal is difficult to exclude and nonrival in reception, satisfying both public-good dimensions.

42231.q: A digital hazard map is initially open, nonrival and free to copy. Verified accounts can enforce a paywall at a real cost. A paywall would finance updates but exclude some users whose benefit exceeds the near-zero cost of serving them. Which evaluation is complete?
options: Adopt the paywall whenever revenue increases, because all lost access represents wasted consumption.
Reject account verification because nonrival information cannot be made excludable.
Treat account enforcement as a change in rivalry rather than a change in feasible exclusion.
Compare the benefit of financed updates with exclusion losses and enforcement costs; better revenue does not alone prove higher welfare.
42231.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
42231.feedback: Technology can make a nonrival service excludable and improve revenue capture. That can support useful updates while also blocking valuable low-cost access and consuming enforcement resources. Net welfare depends on all three effects.

42241.q: A password is shared widely and the provider cannot identify unauthorized users. What limits effective excludability?
options: Authorized use becomes rival automatically
The access rule is difficult to enforce
The service has no marginal cost
The provider is privately owned
42241.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
42241.feedback: A nominal password rule does not create strong exclusion when unauthorized use cannot be detected or stopped.

42253.q: A nonexcludable siren project is worth $300 to each of five households and costs $1,000. One household cannot finance it alone. A binding agreement would collect $200 from each household only if all five sign, with no contracting costs. Which comparison follows?
options: The project is inefficient because no single household values it at its full $1,000 cost.
Uncoordinated funding can fail despite $500 of total gains; the conditional agreement can make every household $100 better off.
The agreement makes the siren rival because every household now pays a fee.
The agreement creates $1,000 of new social benefit solely by collecting contributions.
42253.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
42253.feedback: Total value is 5 x 300 = $1,500, leaving $500 after resource cost. Each household gains 300 - 200 = $100 under the binding agreement. It coordinates contributions without changing the warning’s rivalry or excludability.

42263.q: A neighborhood patrol benefits every home on a block, including households that decline the fee. What is the central financing problem?
options: Protection is consumed by the first household
Fees make the patrol nonrival
The patrol creates open-access depletion
Each household may wait for others to pay for the shared protection
42263.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
42263.feedback: The patrol's nonexcludable benefit gives households an incentive to enjoy protection financed by their neighbors.

42274.q: A nonrival safety bulletin yields $1,500 of total user benefit when open and costs $900 to produce. Donations provide $500. A sponsor would pay $1,000 to keep it open; alternatively, a paywall yields $1,100 of receipts, retains $1,200 of user benefit and costs $100 to enforce. Treat payments as transfers and assume no other effects. Which financing plan is viable and gives larger net social benefit?
options: The paywall: its $1,100 receipts prove greater welfare than the sponsor’s $1,000 payment.
Donations: $1,500 of benefit means the producer can cover costs with $500 of receipts.
Sponsorship: it covers production and preserves $600 of net social benefit, versus $200 under the paywall.
Both paid plans yield identical welfare because information remains nonrival.
42274.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
42274.feedback: Sponsorship receipts cover $900 of cost and leave net social benefit 1500 - 900 = $600. Paywall receipts cover production plus enforcement, but net social benefit is 1200 - 900 - 100 = $200. Revenue feasibility and welfare are separate comparisons.

42285.q: A village’s open fishery is depleted while its nonexcludable flood-warning system receives too few contributions. Leaders propose a catch fee and a collective warning-service fund. Which diagnosis explains why the two remedies target different margins?
options: Both remedies should discourage consumption because fish and warnings are depleted by each user.
The fee discourages rival extraction that harms other users; the fund coordinates payment for a shared nonrival benefit.
Both remedies should subsidize individual use because nonexcludability always causes too little consumption.
The fishery needs only voluntary donations, while the warning requires a catch-style quantity quota.
42285.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42285.feedback: The fishery combines difficult exclusion with rival use, encouraging excessive extraction. The warning is nonrival and nonexcludable, encouraging underpayment and underprovision. Similar access problems need different incentives because rivalry differs.

P52B-MFAIL-B2-002.q: Why might a public good be underprovided privately?
options: Use by one person prevents all others from using it.
People can benefit without paying, weakening voluntary funding.
Exclusion is effortless.
Every consumer reveals exact willingness to pay.
P52B-MFAIL-B2-002.commonError: Misidentifying the source of market failure.
P52B-MFAIL-B2-002.feedback: When nonpayers can benefit from the good, individuals have an incentive to free ride, so voluntary private funding can be below the efficient level.

42160.q: Refer to the emergency-sirens graph. At what quantity do MSB and MC intersect?
options: 40 sirens
20 sirens
30 sirens
60 sirens
42160.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
42160.feedback: MSB intersects MC at 40 sirens, so the marginal social benefit of the 40th siren equals its marginal cost.

42161.q: Refer to the graph. At the efficient emergency-siren quantity, what marginal benefit and marginal cost are shown?
options: $10,000 per siren
$20,000 per siren
$30,000 per siren
$40,000 per siren
42161.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
42161.feedback: At 40 sirens, the graph shows 20 on an axis measured in thousands of dollars per siren, so MSB and MC both equal $20,000 per siren.

42162.q: Suppose the community currently has 30 emergency sirens. What does the graph imply about one more siren?
options: Its marginal cost exceeds its marginal social benefit
Its marginal social benefit is zero
Its marginal social benefit exceeds its marginal cost
Its provision cannot affect net social benefit
42162.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
42162.feedback: At 30 sirens, the graph shows MSB of $25,000 and MC of $20,000. Another siren adds more social benefit than cost, so expanding provision raises net social benefit.
42162.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.
42162.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

42163.q: If 50 emergency sirens have been installed, which marginal comparison follows from the graph?
options: MSB exceeds MC, so the system is underprovided
MSB equals MC, so 50 is efficient
Private Benefit exceeds MSB
MC exceeds MSB, so the last sirens are overprovided
42163.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
42163.feedback: At 50 sirens, the graph shows MSB of $15,000 and MC of $20,000. Marginal cost exceeds marginal social benefit, indicating provision beyond the efficient 40 sirens.

42164.q: Refer to the graph. Why is 40, rather than the largest displayed quantity, the efficient number of sirens?
options: The 40th siren is the point where MSB equals MC
Every resident buys exactly one siren at 40
Total benefit becomes zero at 40
Marginal cost is minimized only at 40
42164.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
42164.feedback: The graph places the MSB-MC intersection at 40 sirens. Beyond that point, an additional siren's cost exceeds its added social benefit even though total benefit remains positive.
42164.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.

42165.q: Refer to the graph. At 20 emergency sirens, what value does the MSB curve show?
options: $10,000 per siren
$30,000 per siren
$20,000 per siren
$40,000 per siren
42165.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
42165.feedback: At Q = 20, the MSB curve is at 30 on an axis measured in thousands of dollars per siren, so marginal social benefit is $30,000 per siren.
42165.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.
42165.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

42167.q: Which statement best describes the MC curve in the emergency-sirens graph?
options: Total siren cost is fixed at $20,000
Marginal cost falls by $500 per siren
Only the first siren has a cost
Each additional siren costs $20,000 over the shown range
42167.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
42167.feedback: The horizontal MC curve is at 20 on an axis measured in thousands of dollars per siren, so each additional siren costs $20,000; total cost is not fixed.

42167.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

42168.q: The siren system warns all residents at once and an additional listener does not reduce the warning available to others. Which feature does that illustrate?
options: Nonrivalry in consumption
Rivalry among suppliers
Excludability through pricing
Depletion of a common resource
42168.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42168.feedback: The warning reaches additional residents without reducing the warning available to anyone else, so consumption is nonrival under the stated conditions.

42170.q: In the local-public-radio graph, where does the Private Benefit curve intersect MC?
options: 20 hours per week
60 hours per week
40 hours per week
80 hours per week
42170.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
42170.feedback: Private Benefit equals MC at 40 hours, identifying the quantity supported by the revealed private incentive in this pure-public-good setting.
42170.imageAlt: Local public radio graph: Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours and MSB intersects MC at 80 hours per week.

MSB equals 100 minus Q, Private Benefit equals 60 minus Q, and MC equals 20. Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours; MSB intersects MC at 80 hours.

42172.q: Based on the two intersections shown in the graph, how much lower is private provision than efficient provision?
options: 40 hours per week
20 hours per week
60 hours per week
80 hours per week
42172.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
42172.feedback: Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours while MSB intersects MC at 80 hours. The underprovision gap is 80 - 40 = 40 hours.
42172.imageAlt: Local public radio graph: Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours and MSB intersects MC at 80 hours per week.

42174.q: Refer to the graph. At 40 hours of local public radio, what is MSB?
options: $2,000 per hour
$4,000 per hour
$6,000 per hour
$8,000 per hour
42174.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
42174.feedback: At Q = 40, the graph shows MSB at 60 on an axis measured in hundreds of dollars per hour, so marginal social benefit is $6,000 per hour. MC is $2,000 per hour.

MSB equals 100 minus Q, Private Benefit equals 60 minus Q, and MC equals 20. Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours; MSB intersects MC at 80 hours.

42177.q: For nonexcludable radio programming, which change could let a private organization provide more programming despite free riding?
options: Making the signal more nonexcludable
A sponsorship contract that pays for audience-wide benefits
Ignoring benefits to noncontributors
Assuming every listener voluntarily reveals full willingness to pay
42177.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
42177.feedback: A sponsorship contract supplies an alternative revenue mechanism that can capture some audience-wide benefit even when nonpayers cannot be excluded from the signal.

P77-MFAIL-LB-029.q: A nonrival, nonexcludable water-quality alert system would generate $12,000 in total benefits and cost $8,000 to operate. Individual fee collection would cost $5,000; a binding cooperative funding agreement would cost $1,000. Both could fund the same service. Which evaluation is correct if there are no other effects?
options: Individual collection creates $4,000 of net gains because collection uses no resources.
The cooperative creates $3,000 of net gains; individual collection costs exceed the $4,000 operating surplus.
Both methods create $12,000 of net gains because users benefit whether or not they pay.
Neither can work because a private agreement cannot finance a nonexcludable service.
P77-MFAIL-LB-029.commonError: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
P77-MFAIL-LB-029.feedback: Before funding costs the gain is 12,000 - 8,000 = $4,000. Net gains are -$1,000 with individual collection and $3,000 with the agreement. Nonexcludability complicates funding but does not rule out every institution.

P77-MFAIL-LB-031.q: A fishery’s paper quota is strict, but hidden catches make actual harvest high. A feasible alternative combines verified landing reports with transferable catch rights. What evidence would establish that this alternative improves net social benefit?
options: The new quota is numerically smaller, regardless of hidden catches or enforcement costs.
Quota holders receive valuable rights, so their transfer income equals the total welfare gain.
Trading occurs frequently, so actual harvest must equal the legally allowed total.
Reduced depletion losses exceed added monitoring and adjustment costs, while transfers permit lower-cost compliance.
P77-MFAIL-LB-031.commonError: Treating identified failure as proof that any intervention is superior.
P77-MFAIL-LB-031.feedback: Evaluate actual behavior, not just the announced cap. Verification can reduce hidden harvest; transfers can lower compliance costs. Net improvement requires avoided resource losses to exceed real implementation and adjustment costs.

42169.q: Refer to the sirens graph, treating provision as continuous. A proposal installs 60 rather than the quantity that maximizes net social benefit. What excess provision and loss follow, and can positive total benefits alone justify the proposal?
options: 20 excess sirens and $400,000 of lost net benefit; every dollar spent on them is a net loss.
20 excess sirens and $100,000 of lost net benefit; positive total benefits do not establish that the extra sirens are worthwhile.
40 excess sirens and $200,000 of lost net benefit; the marginal-cost value is the target quantity.
No excess provision; any quantity with positive MSB maximizes net social benefit.
42169.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
42169.feedback: MSB = MC at 40. From 40 to 60, the gap MC - MSB rises from 0 to $10,000 per siren. The excess-loss triangle is 0.5 x 20 x 10,000 = $100,000. Extra sirens may have positive benefit while costing even more.
42169.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.
42169.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

42179.q: Refer to the public-radio graph. A fund can raise provision from the quantity supported by Private Benefit to the MSB-MC intersection. It uses $10,000 per week in real administration costs; transfers themselves have no resource cost. Which conclusion is supported?
options: The expansion loses $10,000 because donations already measure the full social marginal benefit.
The expansion gains $150,000 because the entire benefit gap is a rectangle.
The expansion gains $80,000 net because administration is a transfer rather than a resource cost.
The expansion yields $70,000 of net weekly gains; voluntary payments alone omit some beneficiaries’ value.
42179.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
42179.feedback: Private Benefit supports 40 hours; MSB meets MC at 80. The MSB-MC gap falls from $4,000 per hour at 40 to zero at 80. Gross gains are 0.5 x 40 x 4,000 = $80,000; after $10,000 administration they are $70,000.
42179.imageAlt: Local public radio graph: Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours and MSB intersects MC at 80 hours per week.
42179.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is hours of local public radio programming per week. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in hundreds of dollars per hour. MSB equals 100 minus Q, Private Benefit equals 60 minus Q, and MC equals 20. Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours; MSB intersects MC at 80 hours.

42189.q: Refer to the coastal-protection graph and treat quantity as continuous. A council budgets $700 million to expand from 10 to 30 miles. With no fixed or financing costs, which assessment uses the changing marginal cost correctly?
options: The expansion costs $400 million because its initial marginal cost applies to all 20 miles.
The budget is sufficient: expansion costs $500 million and adds $300 million in net benefits.
The expansion costs $600 million because its final marginal cost applies to all 20 miles.
The budget is insufficient because the $800 million added benefit must also be paid as cost.
42189.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
42189.feedback: MC rises from $20 million to $30 million per mile, so added cost is 20 x (20 + 30)/2 = $500 million. MSB falls from 50 to 30, giving added benefit 20 x (50 + 30)/2 = $800 million. Net gain is $300 million.
42189.imageAlt: Coastal flood protection graph with downward-sloping MSB and upward-sloping MC intersecting at 30 miles and $30 million per mile.
42189.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is miles of coastal flood protection. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in millions of dollars per mile. MSB equals 60 minus Q and MC equals 15 plus 0.5Q. They intersect at 30 miles, where both equal $30 million per mile.

42199.q: Refer to the fireworks graph and treat displays as continuous. Suppose a proposal uses only North’s willingness to pay to decide provision. What quantity and welfare loss result compared with using both neighborhoods’ benefits, ignoring funding costs?
options: Four displays and no welfare loss, because the larger neighborhood represents everyone.
Zero displays and $200,000 of forgone net benefits, equal to the full cost of four displays.
Eight displays and $20,000 of forgone benefits, because neighborhood quantities should be added.
Zero displays and $80,000 of forgone net benefits.
42199.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42199.feedback: North MB equals MC only at Q = 0 and is below MC for positive quantities. Summed MSB starts $40,000 above MC and meets MC at Q = 4. Omitting all four displays loses the triangle 0.5 x 4 x 40,000 = $80,000.
42199.imageAlt: Community fireworks graph with North MB, South MB, vertically summed MSB, and MC, with decomposition guides at four displays.
42199.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is community fireworks displays per summer. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per display. North MB is max of zero and 50 minus 5Q. South MB is max of zero and 40 minus 5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $50,000 per display. At four displays, North MB is $30,000, South MB is $20,000, and MSB equals MC at $50,000.

P52B-MFAIL-R-002.q: A public good is defined by:
options: Government ownership alone.
Nonrival consumption and difficulty excluding nonpayers.
A high market price.
Private benefits only.
P52B-MFAIL-R-002.commonError: Using the provider rather than the good’s characteristics.
P52B-MFAIL-R-002.feedback: Public-good status depends on rivalry and excludability.

42242.q: Which question should a student ask first when deciding whether a service is excludable?
options: How many firms sell it?
Does government approve it?
Can nonpayers feasibly be prevented from receiving it?
Is its total benefit positive?
42242.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
42242.feedback: Excludability is about feasible denial of access to nonpayers, not legality, supplier competition, or total social benefit.

42252.q: A shared resource is described as rival. What evidence would support that description?
options: Each user's consumption leaves less quantity or quality for others
Users can be charged a membership fee
Several suppliers advertise it
The resource is socially valuable
42252.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
42252.feedback: Rival consumption means one user's activity reduces the quantity or quality available to other users.

42267.q: A student says free riding means 'people are bad.' What is the more precise economic explanation?
options: Public goods eliminate incentives
Free riding requires theft
Nonrivalry means only one person benefits
Nonexcludability allows a person to benefit without bearing the contribution cost
42267.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
42267.feedback: The mechanism is an incentive created by nonexcludability: an individual can receive the benefit while shifting payment to others.

42277.q: What is the precise private-provision concern for a pure nonexcludable public good?
options: Private firms are legally barred from production
Market revenue may fall short of the social value created
Marginal social benefit is always zero
Every unit is overused like a common resource
42277.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
42277.feedback: When beneficiaries can receive the good without paying, the provider cannot capture all willingness to pay, so profitable output may be below efficient provision.

P52B-MFAIL-BR-001.q: A shared office kitchen is repeatedly left dirty because each worker expects others to clean it. This resembles:
options: A common-resource or collective-action problem.
A perfectly enforced private property right.
A positive price signal.
A competitive firm’s shutdown decision.
P52B-MFAIL-BR-001.commonError: Failing to transfer shared-resource incentives to everyday settings.
P52B-MFAIL-BR-001.feedback: Shared access and dispersed responsibility can encourage overuse or under-maintenance.

P77-MFAIL-BR-039.q: A public-good rule changes incentives to contribute. What connection matters?
options: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
It is rival with fully enforceable private access
Free-riding incentives can reduce voluntary provision
It is a private good supplied by government
P77-MFAIL-BR-039.commonError: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
P77-MFAIL-BR-039.feedback: Because nonpayers can still benefit from a public good, contribution rules affect free-riding incentives and therefore voluntary provision.

42209.q: A free public beach becomes crowded enough that each visitor has less space. What changed?
options: The beach became excludable without an access rule
Consumption became rival at the congested level
Firm rivalry increased
Nonpayers became easier to identify automatically
42209.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
42209.feedback: Crowding means another visitor reduces the quality or space available to others, so use becomes rival even though access remains difficult to exclude.

42228.q: A paid satellite weather feed can deny access to noncustomers and can serve another subscriber without using up the forecast. What is it?
options: Club good
Public good
Private good
Common resource
42228.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
42228.feedback: Encryption makes the feed excludable and the information is nonrival over the stated range, so it is a club good.

42303.q: A common resource is being overused. What is the key private-social gap?
options: Users omit all of their own benefit
The resource is nonrival
The supplier cannot calculate marginal revenue
Users omit part of the depletion or congestion cost imposed on others
42303.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
42303.feedback: Open-access users capture much of their private benefit but do not bear the full cost their rival use imposes on others.

42319.q: Why can property or access rights improve common-resource efficiency?
options: They make the resource nonrival
They guarantee zero transaction cost
They remove every competing use
They make users bear more of the opportunity cost of depletion
42319.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
42319.feedback: Enforceable rights connect current use with forgone future value or lost use by others, reducing the incentive for open-access overuse.

ECON-MG-EASY-14.q: A seller with substantial influence over the market price has:
options: A price ceiling
A PPF
A circular flow
Market power
ECON-MG-EASY-14.feedback: Market power exists when a buyer or seller can influence price.

P77-MFAIL-E-005.q: A seller can profitably influence price by restricting output. What concern appears?
options: A negative externality imposed on third parties
A public-good free-rider problem
A common-resource overuse problem.
Market power
P77-MFAIL-E-005.commonError: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
P77-MFAIL-E-005.feedback: Market power can restrict mutually beneficial trades by influencing price or quantity.

ECON-MG-MEDIUM-107.q: A market has one dominant seller that can influence price. Why might the market outcome be inefficient?
options: Scarcity disappears when one seller dominates
Market power can distort price and quantity
Opportunity cost no longer applies
The dominant seller must produce the efficient quantity.
ECON-MG-MEDIUM-107.feedback: Market power can allow a seller to influence price and reduce market efficiency.

P77-MFAIL-M-009.q: A dominant platform blocks entry and reduces trades. What is the core concern?
options: Blocking entry makes the platform nonexcludable
Reducing trades creates a public-good free-rider problem
The platform’s size by itself proves a negative externality.
Market power can keep quantity below the efficient level
P77-MFAIL-M-009.commonError: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
P77-MFAIL-M-009.feedback: Market power can restrict mutually beneficial trades by influencing price or quantity.

P52B-MFAIL-H-003.q: A dominant seller withholds an additional unit that a buyer values at $25 even though producing it uses $18 of resources. There are no externalities. Which mechanism explains the lost efficiency?
options: The withheld trade creates a $7 external pollution cost paid by a third party.
The seller’s lost sales revenue equals the social gain, regardless of production cost.
Restricting output can preserve the seller’s price while forgoing a trade with $7 of social gains.
Any price above resource cost proves that expanding output would reduce total surplus.
P52B-MFAIL-H-003.commonError: Treating market power as only a distributional issue.
P52B-MFAIL-H-003.feedback: The omitted unit has willingness to pay above marginal resource cost by 25 - 18 = $7. Market power can make restricting output privately attractive even though the unit would add social surplus. No third-party spillover is required.

P52B-MFAIL-L-003.q: A broadband network has high fixed cost and low marginal cost. Marginal-cost pricing would expand valuable access but leave a financing deficit. Average-cost pricing can cover costs but excludes some users whose value exceeds marginal cost. Public support has a real collection cost. What information is needed to choose between the two rules?
options: Only whether marginal-cost pricing creates an accounting loss, because loss proves social inefficiency.
Only whether average-cost pricing breaks even, because break-even proves maximum social surplus.
The extra access benefits net of resource cost, compared with the real cost of financing the deficit.
Only the subsidy payment, because every transferred dollar is a destroyed social resource.
P52B-MFAIL-L-003.commonError: Ignoring the pricing and cost-recovery tradeoff.
P52B-MFAIL-L-003.feedback: The financing problem and the access distortion are distinct. Compare additional gains from valuable access with financing’s real costs under feasible support arrangements. Accounting losses and transfer amounts do not alone rank the rules.

P77-MFAIL-L-020.q: An exclusive right lets an innovator charge above marginal cost. Removing it would expand current access but could reduce future investment in similar products. Which evidence is needed before claiming removal raises welfare?
options: Only the current markup, because all markups equal net profit and total social loss.
Only the innovator’s revenue, because consumer gains are transfers that cannot affect welfare.
Only the number of new buyers, because future incentives are unrelated to exclusive rights.
Gains from additional current trades and the size of any resulting loss of valuable future innovation.
P77-MFAIL-L-020.commonError: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
P77-MFAIL-L-020.feedback: Market power can exclude mutually beneficial current purchases, while expected returns can affect investment. A welfare comparison needs both margins and cannot be settled by the markup or seller revenue alone. This asks about incentives, not a legal test.

P52B-MFAIL-B2-003.q: What is the standard efficiency concern with market power?
options: Every firm earns zero accounting profit.
All prices fall below marginal cost.
Output may be restricted below the level where buyer value exceeds production cost.
Products become nonrival when one firm sets the market price.
P52B-MFAIL-B2-003.commonError: Misidentifying the source of market failure.
P52B-MFAIL-B2-003.feedback: Market power can restrict output below the efficient quantity, leaving mutually beneficial trades unrealized and creating deadweight loss.

P77-MFAIL-R-036.q: How does market power differ from an externality?
options: Market power requires a third-party spillover outside the transaction
It influences market terms rather than imposing a third-party spillover
Market power makes the good nonrival and nonexcludable
Market power occurs only when income is distributed unequally.
P77-MFAIL-R-036.commonError: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
P77-MFAIL-R-036.feedback: Market power can restrict mutually beneficial trades by influencing price or quantity.

externalities.title: Externalities
externalities.description: Analyze positive and negative externalities, social and private margins, corrective policies, private solutions, and Coase bargaining.

A negative externality
A perfectly efficient market
A positive externality.
easy.commonError: confuses_externality_with_private_cost
easy.feedback: Pollution affects bystanders, so it is a negative externality.

A third party bears a cost outside the transaction
A large firm merely changes its own cost
The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
easy.commonError: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
easy.feedback: An externality affects people outside the transaction.
