market-power.title: Market Power
market-power.description: Identify price-setting ability, barriers to entry, restricted output, allocative inefficiency, and deadweight loss from market power.

easy.q: A seller with substantial influence over the market price has:
options: A price ceiling
A PPF
A circular flow
Market power
easy.commonError: confuses_market_power_with_high_demand
easy.feedback: Market power exists when a buyer or seller can influence price.

easy.q: A seller can profitably influence price by restricting output. What concern appears?
options: A negative externality imposed on third parties
A public-good free-rider problem
A common-resource overuse problem.
Market power
easy.commonError: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
easy.feedback: Market power can restrict mutually beneficial trades by influencing price or quantity.

medium.q: A market has one dominant seller that can influence price. Why might the market outcome be inefficient?
options: Scarcity disappears when one seller dominates
Market power can distort price and quantity
Opportunity cost no longer applies
The dominant seller must produce the efficient quantity.
medium.commonError: thinks_market_power_only_means_large_firm_not_distortion
medium.feedback: Market power can allow a seller to influence price and reduce market efficiency.

medium.q: A dominant platform blocks entry and reduces trades. What is the core concern?
options: Blocking entry makes the platform nonexcludable
Reducing trades creates a public-good free-rider problem
The platform’s size by itself proves a negative externality.
Market power can keep quantity below the efficient level
medium.commonError: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
medium.feedback: Market power can restrict mutually beneficial trades by influencing price or quantity.

hard.q: A dominant seller withholds an additional unit that a buyer values at $25 even though producing it uses $18 of resources. There are no externalities. Which mechanism explains the lost efficiency?
options: The withheld trade creates a $7 external pollution cost paid by a third party.
The seller’s lost sales revenue equals the social gain, regardless of production cost.
Restricting output can preserve the seller’s price while forgoing a trade with $7 of social gains.
Any price above resource cost proves that expanding output would reduce total surplus.
hard.commonError: Treating market power as only a distributional issue.
hard.feedback: The omitted unit has willingness to pay above marginal resource cost by 25 - 18 = $7. Market power can make restricting output privately attractive even though the unit would add social surplus. No third-party spillover is required.

legendary.q: A broadband network has high fixed cost and low marginal cost. Marginal-cost pricing would expand valuable access but leave a financing deficit. Average-cost pricing can cover costs but excludes some users whose value exceeds marginal cost. Public support has a real collection cost. What information is needed to choose between the two rules?
options: Only whether marginal-cost pricing creates an accounting loss, because loss proves social inefficiency.
Only whether average-cost pricing breaks even, because break-even proves maximum social surplus.
The extra access benefits net of resource cost, compared with the real cost of financing the deficit.
Only the subsidy payment, because every transferred dollar is a destroyed social resource.
legendary.commonError: Ignoring the pricing and cost-recovery tradeoff.
legendary.feedback: The financing problem and the access distortion are distinct. Compare additional gains from valuable access with financing’s real costs under feasible support arrangements. Accounting losses and transfer amounts do not alone rank the rules.

legendary.q: An exclusive right lets an innovator charge above marginal cost. Removing it would expand current access but could reduce future investment in similar products. Which evidence is needed before claiming removal raises welfare?
options: Only the current markup, because all markups equal net profit and total social loss.
Only the innovator’s revenue, because consumer gains are transfers that cannot affect welfare.
Only the number of new buyers, because future incentives are unrelated to exclusive rights.
Gains from additional current trades and the size of any resulting loss of valuable future innovation.
legendary.commonError: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
legendary.feedback: Market power can exclude mutually beneficial current purchases, while expected returns can affect investment. A welfare comparison needs both margins and cannot be settled by the markup or seller revenue alone. This asks about incentives, not a legal test.

boss.q: What is the standard efficiency concern with market power?
options: Every firm earns zero accounting profit.
All prices fall below marginal cost.
Output may be restricted below the level where buyer value exceeds production cost.
Products become nonrival when one firm sets the market price.
boss.commonError: Misidentifying the source of market failure.
boss.feedback: Market power can restrict output below the efficient quantity, leaving mutually beneficial trades unrealized and creating deadweight loss.

repairQuestions.q: How does market power differ from an externality?
options: Market power requires a third-party spillover outside the transaction
It influences market terms rather than imposing a third-party spillover
Market power makes the good nonrival and nonexcludable
Market power occurs only when income is distributed unequally.
repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
repairQuestions.feedback: Market power can restrict mutually beneficial trades by influencing price or quantity.

easy.q: Pollution from a factory that harms nearby residents is an example of:
options: A price floor
A negative externality
A perfectly efficient market
A positive externality.
easy.commonError: confuses_externality_with_private_cost
easy.feedback: Pollution affects bystanders, so it is a negative externality.

easy.q: A neighbor bears smoke from a restaurant exhaust fan. What feature identifies an externality?
options: The outcome is a public good by definition
A third party bears a cost outside the transaction
A large firm merely changes its own cost
The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
easy.commonError: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
easy.feedback: An externality affects people outside the transaction.

easy.q: Refer to the fast-fashion garments graph. Which type of externality is represented by the private and social marginal curves?
options: Negative production externality
Negative consumption externality
Positive production externality
Positive consumption externality
easy.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
easy.feedback: This is a negative production externality: the activity creates a cost for people outside the market transaction, so the relevant social and private marginal curves differ.
easy.imageAlt: Graph of fast-fashion garments (millions) with labeled marginal curves.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis measures fast-fashion garments (millions), from 0 to 320. The vertical axis measures marginal benefit and cost in dollars per garment. MPB is a straight line from (0, $21) to (320, $9). MPC is a straight line from (0, $3) to (320, $15). MSC is a straight line from (0, $9) to (320, $21), parallel to MPC. No dots, projection guides or brackets are drawn.

easy.q: Based on the fast-fashion garments graph, what economic relationship explains the position of the social curve relative to the private curve?
options: MSC is below MPC because buyers receive an external benefit
MSC is above MPC because production imposes an external cost
MPB is above MSB because production creates a benefit
MPC is above MSC because firms pay every social cost
easy.commonError: Using private curves alone when social costs or benefits determine efficiency.
easy.feedback: MSC is above MPC because production imposes an external cost. The constant vertical separation is the marginal external cost omitted from private decisions.
easy.imageAlt: Graph of fast-fashion garments (millions) with labeled marginal curves.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis measures fast-fashion garments (millions), from 0 to 320. The vertical axis measures marginal benefit and cost in dollars per garment. MPB is a straight line from (0, $21) to (320, $9). MPC is a straight line from (0, $3) to (320, $15). MSC is a straight line from (0, $9) to (320, $21), parallel to MPC. No dots, projection guides or brackets are drawn.

easy.q: If no corrective policy is adopted, how will the market quantity of fast-fashion garments compare with the socially efficient quantity?
options: The market underproduces by 80 million garments
The market is efficient because MPB intersects MPC
The market overproduces by 80 million garments
The market overproduces by 160 million garments
easy.commonError: Using private curves alone when social costs or benefits determine efficiency.
easy.feedback: The unregulated market equilibrium occurs where MPC intersects MPB, at 240 million garments and $12. The socially efficient outcome occurs where MSC intersects MPB, at 160 million garments and $15. The difference is 80 million garments, so the market has overproduction. Private choices omit the external cost.

MPB is a straight line from (0, $16) to (200, $8). MPC is a straight line from (0, $6) to (200, $18). MSC is a straight line from (0, $1) to (200, $13), parallel to MPC. A red dot marks the MPB-MPC intersection at (100, $12); a green dot marks the MPB-MSC intersection at (150, $10). Dashed guides project those dots to the axes.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At what quantity do MPC and MPB intersect in the unregulated market for public-transit rides?
options: 200 thousand rides per day
50 thousand rides per day
150 thousand rides per day
350 thousand rides per day
easy.commonError: Reversing social and private curves or predicting overproduction instead of underproduction.
easy.feedback: The unregulated market equilibrium occurs where MPC intersects MPB, at 150 thousand rides per day and $5.
easy.imageAlt: Graph of public-transit rides (thousands per day) with labeled marginal curves, with intersection guides.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis measures public-transit rides (thousands per day), from 0 to 250. The vertical axis measures marginal benefit and cost in dollars per ride. MPB is a straight line from (0, $8) to (250, $3). MPC is a straight line from (0, $2) to (250, $7). MSB is a straight line from (0, $10) to (250, $5), parallel to MPB. A red dot marks the MPB-MPC intersection at (150, $5); a green dot marks the MSB-MPC intersection at (200, $6). Dashed guides project those dots to the axes.

easy.q: A steel mill's smoke harms nearby households. Which classification is most precise?
options: Negative production externality
Negative consumption externality
Positive production externality
Positive consumption externality
easy.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
easy.feedback: Production imposes a third-party cost. Because the smoke is created during production, the omitted harm raises marginal social cost above the mill's private marginal cost.

easy.q: Secondhand smoke from using a product harms restaurant patrons. What kind of spillover is this?
options: Negative production externality
Negative consumption externality
Positive production externality
Positive consumption externality
easy.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
easy.feedback: The harmful spillover follows consumption. The purchase itself is not the spillover; the harm generated when the product is consumed falls on people outside the transaction.

easy.q: A beekeeper's hives improve nearby orchard yields without payment. How is the effect classified?
options: Negative production externality
Negative consumption externality
Positive production externality
Positive consumption externality
easy.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
easy.feedback: Production by the beekeeper creates an external benefit. The beekeeper does not capture all of the added orchard output, so the social benefit of producing hives exceeds the private benefit.

easy.q: A vaccination reduces infection risk for people other than the patient. What is the spillover?
options: Negative consumption externality
Negative production externality
Positive production externality
Positive consumption externality
easy.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
easy.feedback: Consuming the vaccination benefits third parties. The patient receives a private benefit, while reduced transmission creates an additional social benefit for other people.

easy.q: A landscaping company creates noise while serving a customer. Which channel creates the externality?
options: Production
Consumption
A public-good channel
A price-control channel
easy.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
easy.feedback: The spillover is created while the service is produced. The customer and landscaper are the transacting parties, while nearby residents experience a cost created by the production process.

easy.q: A driver's use of a congested road delays other drivers. Which description is best?
options: A positive production externality
A negative consumption externality
A private cost borne only by the driver
A positive consumption externality
easy.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
easy.feedback: Road use imposes delay on other users. Each trip adds congestion delays for other road users, so the driver's private cost understates the social cost of road use.

easy.q: A rule requires factories to install a verified scrubber. What policy type is this?
options: A corrective consumer subsidy
A tradable-permit market
Command-and-control technology regulation
A private Coase bargain
easy.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
easy.feedback: The rule mandates a technology. Because the regulator specifies the equipment rather than a price or emissions allowance, firms cannot choose a different compliance technology.

easy.q: A city caps each plant's sulfur emissions at 20 tons. What instrument is used?
options: A consumption subsidy
An unregulated permit market
A price floor on output
An emissions standard
easy.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
easy.feedback: A legal maximum emissions amount is a standard. The legal maximum directly constrains each plant's emissions quantity; it does not create a subsidy or a tradable right by itself.

easy.q: Education benefits employers and neighbors beyond the student. What quantity tendency can result?
options: Underconsumption relative to social optimum
Overconsumption
No efficiency effect
A binding price floor
easy.commonError: Reversing social and private curves or predicting overproduction instead of underproduction.
easy.feedback: Private marginal benefit can lie below social marginal benefit. Because consumers count only their private return, MPB lies below MSB and the private market stops before all socially worthwhile units are consumed.

easy.q: A per-unit subsidy equals vaccination's marginal external benefit. What is intended?
options: Reduce vaccination below market quantity
Leave private incentives unchanged
Increase vaccination toward socially efficient quantity
Turn benefit into external cost
easy.commonError: Confusing subsidy expenditure with external benefit or taxing a positive externality.
easy.feedback: The subsidy raises private incentive by the external benefit. By rewarding the external benefit, the subsidy raises the consumer's effective private incentive and moves the MPB-based choice toward the MSB-based efficient quantity.

easy.q: A public good is usually:
options: Always sold by one monopoly firm
A legal maximum price
Hard to exclude people from and shared by many users
A substitute for every other good
easy.commonError: confuses_public_good_with_government_provided_good
easy.feedback: Public goods are generally nonexcludable and nonrival.

easy.q: A storm-warning signal can serve another listener without reducing its value and nonpayers are hard to exclude. What is it?
options: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
It is a private good supplied by government
A public good
It is nonrival but easy to exclude
easy.commonError: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
easy.feedback: Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude.

easy.q: Why is it too strong to claim that private firms can never participate in public-radio provision?
options: Advertising, contracts, donations, or government purchasing can create revenue
Nonexcludability guarantees subscription revenue
MC disappears for private firms
Private Benefit must always equal MSB
easy.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
easy.feedback: Alternative institutions can finance private participation even when direct listener payments understate social benefit. The underprovision result is conditional, not a claim that private participation is impossible.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At 20 miles of coastal protection, which marginal comparison is correct?
options: MSB exceeds MC, so expanding protection raises net social benefit
MC exceeds MSB, so protection should contract
MSB equals MC, so 20 miles is efficient
Private Benefit is necessarily zero
easy.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
easy.feedback: At Q = 20, the graph shows MSB at $40 million and MC at $25 million. The next mile adds more benefit than cost.
easy.imageAlt: Coastal flood protection graph with downward-sloping MSB and upward-sloping MC intersecting at 30 miles and $30 million per mile.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is miles of coastal flood protection. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in millions of dollars per mile. MSB equals 60 minus Q and MC equals 15 plus 0.5Q. They intersect at 30 miles, where both equal $30 million per mile.

easy.q: Community-wide coastal protection can serve another resident without reducing protection for anyone else. Which characteristic does that illustrate?
options: Each protected resident removes protection from another
Only one buyer can consume each mile
Many residents receive the same protection without using it up
Open harvesting depletes the barrier
easy.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
easy.feedback: Flood protection is nonrival over the stated range because protecting another resident does not subtract protection from others.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At four displays, what marginal social benefit results from vertically summing North and South?
easy.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
easy.feedback: At Q = 4, North MB is $30,000 and South MB is $20,000. Because both consume the same display, the benefits add vertically to MSB of $50,000.
easy.imageAlt: Community fireworks graph with North MB, South MB, vertically summed MSB, and MC, with decomposition guides at four displays.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is community fireworks displays per summer. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per display. North MB is max of zero and 50 minus 5Q. South MB is max of zero and 40 minus 5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $50,000 per display. At four displays, North MB is $30,000, South MB is $20,000, and MSB equals MC at $50,000.

easy.q: Refer to the public-radio summation graph. At 40 hours, what is Group A's marginal benefit?
options: $3,000 per hour
$1,000 per hour
$2,000 per hour
$5,000 per hour
easy.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
easy.feedback: At Q = 40, the graph shows Group A's MB at 30 on an axis measured in hundreds of dollars, or $3,000 per hour.
easy.imageAlt: Public radio vertical-summation graph with Group A MB, Group B MB, MSB, and MC, highlighting 40 hours per week.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is hours of local public radio programming per week. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in hundreds of dollars per hour. Group A MB is max of zero and 50 minus 0.5Q. Group B MB is max of zero and 30 minus 0.5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $3,000 per hour. At 40 hours, Group A MB is $3,000 per hour, Group B MB is $1,000 per hour, and MSB is $4,000 per hour.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Which calculation would misread the shared quantity at 40 hours?
options: Adding Group A's 40 hours to Group B's 40 hours to claim 80 hours
Adding marginal benefits of $3,000 and $1,000
Reporting MSB of $4,000 per hour
Recognizing both groups receive 40 hours
easy.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
easy.feedback: Public-good beneficiaries share one common quantity. Their marginal benefits are added vertically; their identical consumed quantities are not added together.
easy.imageAlt: Public radio vertical-summation graph with Group A MB, Group B MB, MSB, and MC, highlighting 40 hours per week.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is hours of local public radio programming per week. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in hundreds of dollars per hour. Group A MB is max of zero and 50 minus 0.5Q. Group B MB is max of zero and 30 minus 0.5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $3,000 per hour. At 40 hours, Group A MB is $3,000 per hour, Group B MB is $1,000 per hour, and MSB is $4,000 per hour.

easy.q: A winter coat is sold to one customer and cannot be worn by another customer at the same time. What category fits?
options: Public good
Common resource
Club good
Private good
easy.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
easy.feedback: The seller can exclude nonbuyers, and one person's use prevents simultaneous use by another, so the coat is excludable and rival.

easy.q: A university database requires a paid login, and simultaneous users do not reduce the information available to one another. Which category fits?
options: Public good
Private good
Common resource
Club good
easy.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
easy.feedback: The login permits exclusion of nonmembers, while digital access is nonrival under the stated capacity conditions.

easy.q: Anyone may fish in a lake, but each catch leaves fewer fish for other anglers. How should the fishery be classified?
options: Public good
Common resource
Private good
Club good
easy.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
easy.feedback: Open access makes exclusion difficult, while catches deplete the stock available to others, so the resource is nonexcludable and rival.

easy.q: A research archive places its digital articles behind a paywall, and additional readers do not reduce access quality. What category applies?
options: Public good
Club good
Private good
Common resource
easy.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
easy.feedback: The paywall makes the archive excludable, while digital reading is nonrival over the stated capacity range.

easy.q: A lake has no fences, permits, or patrols. Which fact most directly supports nonexcludability?
options: Preventing unapproved users from reaching the lake is impractical
Fish are scarce
Anglers compete in tournaments
The lake has measurable depth
easy.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
easy.feedback: Nonexcludability concerns the feasibility of denying access, not whether the resource is scarce or whether users compete.

easy.q: A toll transponder is required to enter a bridge. What is the direct economic effect of the transponder system?
options: It creates a practical way to exclude nonpayers
It guarantees the bridge is uncongested
It makes each crossing nonrival
It eliminates maintenance costs
easy.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
easy.feedback: The transponder controls access and makes exclusion feasible. Congestion determines rivalry separately.

easy.q: One commuter occupies the last seat on a bus. What does this show?
options: The seat is nonrival because the bus follows a route
The seat is excludable only if government owns it
The seat reflects rivalry among bus companies
The seat is rival because it is unavailable to another commuter
easy.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
easy.feedback: A seat used by one passenger cannot simultaneously serve another, so consumption of that seat is rival.

easy.q: Why is groundwater rival in consumption?
options: Groundwater users compete in product markets
The aquifer can never be fenced
Water has a positive price
Water pumped by one user reduces the stock available to others
easy.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
easy.feedback: Rivalry follows from depletion: one user's withdrawal leaves less groundwater for other users.

easy.q: A household understates how much it values flood protection during a voluntary fundraising survey. What motive may explain the response?
options: It wants the barrier to become rival
It cannot benefit if another household pays
It hopes to lower its payment while still receiving protection
It is revealing the full social benefit
easy.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
easy.feedback: Because protection reaches the household even if it contributes little, understating willingness to pay can reduce its expected share of the cost.

easy.q: Which statement best distinguishes a free rider from someone who receives no benefit?
options: A free rider pays but cannot consume
A free rider depletes an open-access resource
A free rider benefits but does not pay or contribute
A free rider always breaks a law
easy.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
easy.feedback: Free riding requires receiving a benefit without contributing toward its cost; a person who receives no benefit is not riding on others' provision.

easy.q: Why can a unanimous claim that 'someone else will fund it' be self-defeating for a public good?
options: If everyone withholds payment, a valued project may not be provided
Withholding makes MSB equal zero
The project becomes rival
The project is necessarily overprovided
easy.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
easy.feedback: Individually attractive free riding can produce a collective outcome in which contributions are too small to finance a project whose total social benefit exceeds cost.

easy.q: Which statement about private firms and public goods is economically accurate?
options: Private firms never provide anything nonrival
Private firms can participate when contracts, advertising, donations, or public purchasing create revenue
Profit requires every good to be rival
Government ownership is part of the definition of a public good
easy.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
easy.feedback: The underprovision result is conditional, not absolute. Alternative revenue arrangements can support private production even when direct exclusion of beneficiaries is difficult.

easy.q: A charitable foundation pays for open scientific data. Which conclusion is best?
options: The data become rival because a foundation paid
The data are a private good because funding is private
Free riding is impossible whenever donors exist
A private organization can finance a public good without charging each user
easy.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
easy.feedback: Foundation funding is an alternative financing mechanism. The open data can remain nonexcludable and nonrival even though a private organization pays for them.

easy.q: Which challenge arises when benefits from flood protection occur decades in the future?
options: Future and uncertain benefits must be estimated and compared with current costs
Future benefits are automatically zero
Marginal cost stops mattering
The project becomes a private good
easy.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
easy.feedback: Long horizons require forecasts and comparison of benefits and costs occurring at different times, adding uncertainty to valuation.

easy.q: Farmers pumping from a shared aquifer ignore how their withdrawals raise future pumping costs for neighbors. What is the likely outcome?
options: Groundwater is underprovided like a public good
The aquifer becomes nonrival
Groundwater is withdrawn faster than is socially efficient
Every farmer automatically conserves the efficient amount
easy.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
easy.feedback: Each farmer captures the crop benefit while sharing depletion and pumping-cost effects with others, encouraging aggregate withdrawal above the efficient level.

easy.q: A forest is open to unrestricted fuelwood harvesting. Which pattern signals tragedy-of-the-commons pressure?
options: Households pay owners for every tree
New trees are nonrival
Each household harvests without accounting for reduced timber available to others
A single owner bears the full future loss
easy.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
easy.feedback: Open access and rival harvesting let households capture fuelwood benefits while shifting part of the stock loss to other users.

easy.q: A city adds road capacity and congestion briefly falls, but free access attracts more trips. Which risk remains?
options: Capacity makes road space permanently nonrival
Drivers become excludable without a toll
Untolled access can again produce excessive use at congested times
The road becomes a pure public good at every quantity
easy.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
easy.feedback: Additional capacity can delay congestion, but when use is free at the margin drivers still omit delay imposed on others and overuse can return.

easy.q: What would an efficient common-resource rule try to make users consider?
options: The opportunity cost their use imposes on other users
Only their private benefit
Only historical average cost
Whether the resource is publicly named
easy.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
easy.feedback: Efficiency requires users to compare private benefit with the full social opportunity cost, including depletion or congestion imposed on others.

easy.q: Why might voluntary promises alone fail to protect a large open-access forest?
options: The forest is nonrival
Promises automatically create enforceable ownership
Each user can gain by harvesting while relying on others to restrain themselves
Conservation has no social benefit
easy.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
easy.feedback: Without monitoring or enforceable access rules, an individual can privately benefit from violating restraint while the stock cost is dispersed.

easy.q: Which policy logic directly addresses common-resource overuse?
options: Limit or price access so users face more of the depletion or congestion cost
Subsidize every additional unit of use
Make the resource less excludable
Ignore aggregate use and track only private benefit
easy.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
easy.feedback: Access limits, user charges, or enforceable rights connect individual choices more closely to the social cost of using a rival shared resource.

easy.q: Why can common-resource use exceed the efficient quantity even when every user understands depletion?
options: Information automatically removes the incentive
Understanding makes the resource nonrival
Each user may still capture a private gain while bearing only part of the shared cost
Efficiency requires zero resource use
easy.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
easy.feedback: Knowledge alone does not align incentives. A user's private gain can exceed the personal share of depletion cost even when the full social cost is larger.

easy.q: What is required for a legal property right to change resource-use incentives?
options: The resource must become nonrival
The right must be sufficiently clear and enforceable
All transaction costs must be zero
Every user must value the resource equally
easy.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
easy.feedback: Users respond to rights when boundaries and permissions are clear and violations can be detected and sanctioned.

easy.q: Why might a private forest owner conserve young trees?
options: Ownership makes harvesting nonrival
The owner cannot exclude trespassers
Conservation always has zero current cost
Future timber value is part of the owner's private opportunity cost of harvesting now
easy.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
easy.feedback: Secure ownership lets the owner capture future forest value, so cutting a young tree carries a private cost that open-access harvesters may ignore.

easy.q: A toll is introduced on a congested road. How can this improve resource-use incentives?
options: Drivers face a price connected to scarce road capacity and delay
The toll makes road space unlimited
The toll guarantees no congestion at any price
Drivers stop receiving private trip benefits
easy.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
easy.feedback: A toll can make access excludable and require drivers to consider more of the congestion cost associated with scarce road space.

easy.q: Which claim about assigning property rights is too strong?
options: Enforcement matters
Property rights automatically produce perfect efficiency in every setting
Monitoring can be costly
Rights can improve conservation incentives
easy.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
easy.feedback: Rights can align incentives, but unclear boundaries, weak enforcement, ecological spillovers, market power, and transaction costs can prevent a perfect outcome.

easy.q: An exclusive grazing lease is never monitored, and outsiders continue using the land. What is the main problem?
options: Grazing has become nonrival
The lease creates free riding on a public good
The right is not effectively enforceable
Ownership eliminates the need for boundaries
easy.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
easy.feedback: A paper lease does not create practical exclusion when unauthorized grazing cannot be detected or stopped.

easy.q: How can transferable catch shares reduce a race to fish?
options: Shares eliminate scarcity
Shares make fish nonrival
Shares require every fisher to use identical equipment
Fishers no longer need to capture their allowed share before everyone else
easy.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
easy.feedback: A secure share gives each holder a defined claim, reducing the incentive to race for an unowned portion of the catch.

easy.q: Why can community-managed access rights sometimes improve stewardship?
options: Users who share enforceable rules also retain more of the benefits from conserving the resource
Community rules make depletion impossible
Shared management eliminates rivalry
Local users face no monitoring costs
easy.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
easy.feedback: Collective rights can align use with the group's future resource value when rules and sanctions are credible.

easy.q: A city converts an open parking district into spaces reserved for permit holders. Which characteristic changes most directly?
options: Parking becomes nonrival
Excludability increases
Scarcity disappears
Every permit holder consumes the same space
easy.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
easy.feedback: Permits let the city deny access to nonholders, creating excludability. Rivalry remains because one occupied space is unavailable to another driver.

easy.q: What conservation incentive does a long-term water right create that a one-day extraction race may not?
options: The holder stops valuing current water
The right makes the aquifer nonrival
The holder can benefit from preserving future availability
The right removes all uncertainty
easy.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
easy.feedback: A durable claim lets the holder capture part of the future value created by restraint, bringing future scarcity into today's private decision.

easy.q: Why can defining rights be difficult for migratory wildlife?
options: Wildlife is always nonrival
Property rights require a market price of zero
Migration eliminates social value
The resource crosses boundaries and is costly to monitor
easy.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
easy.feedback: Movement across jurisdictions complicates boundaries, monitoring, and enforcement, limiting how completely rights can create exclusion.

easy.q: A fishing cooperative can exclude outsiders but cannot prevent members from exceeding internal limits. What remains unresolved?
options: Enforcement among authorized users
The fish stock has become nonrival
Outsider exclusion is the only relevant incentive
The cooperative has created a public good
easy.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
easy.feedback: Excluding outsiders helps, but members still need monitored and enforceable use rules to prevent depletion within the group.

easy.q: How do clear rights differ from a general request to conserve?
options: A request makes the resource excludable automatically
Clear rights specify who may use the resource and who bears gains or losses from stewardship
Clear rights eliminate marginal cost
A request guarantees penalties for overuse
easy.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
easy.feedback: Defined rights connect authorized use and future resource value to identifiable decision-makers, while a general request may leave access and consequences diffuse.

easy.q: Which combination is most likely to reduce open-access overuse?
options: Undefined access, no monitoring, and voluntary restraint only
More users with identical extraction incentives
Clear access rights, feasible monitoring, and credible enforcement
A rule that cannot detect violations
easy.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
easy.feedback: Rights alter behavior most reliably when users know the boundaries, compliance can be observed, and violations carry credible consequences.

easy.q: A seller with substantial influence over the market price has:
options: A price ceiling
A PPF
A circular flow
Market power
easy.commonError: confuses_market_power_with_high_demand
easy.feedback: Market power exists when a buyer or seller can influence price.

easy.q: A seller can profitably influence price by restricting output. What concern appears?
options: A negative externality imposed on third parties
A public-good free-rider problem
A common-resource overuse problem.
Market power
easy.commonError: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
easy.feedback: Market power can restrict mutually beneficial trades by influencing price or quantity.

medium.q: A delivery truck creates noise for residents who are not customers. Why is this an externality?
options: The cost falls on third parties outside the delivery exchange
The firm pays for fuel and driver time
Customers receive packages they ordered
The service operates in a city market
medium.commonError: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
medium.feedback: An externality affects people outside the transaction.

medium.q: A factory’s pollution harms nearby residents without compensating them. This is:
options: A public good.
A positive consumption externality.
A negative production externality.
A competitive price signal with no omitted cost.
medium.commonError: Misclassifying an external cost.
medium.feedback: The factory imposes a cost on third parties outside the transaction.

medium.q: Why may a busy road be overused when access is free?
options: Drivers share congestion costs imposed on one another
The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
The outcome is a public good by definition
A large firm merely changes its own cost
medium.commonError: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
medium.feedback: When each driver considers the private benefit of the trip but not the congestion delay imposed on other drivers, road use can exceed the socially efficient level.

medium.q: Based on the vertical distance between the private and social curves, what is the constant marginal external effect for fast-fashion garments?
options: $2 per garment
$4 per garment
$5 per garment
$6 per garment
medium.commonError: Using private curves alone when social costs or benefits determine efficiency.
medium.feedback: The private and social curves remain $6 per garment apart, so each unit creates that amount of marginal external cost.
medium.imageAlt: Graph of fast-fashion garments (millions) with labeled marginal curves.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis measures fast-fashion garments (millions), from 0 to 320. The vertical axis measures marginal benefit and cost in dollars per garment. MPB is a straight line from (0, $21) to (320, $9). MPC is a straight line from (0, $3) to (320, $15). MSC is a straight line from (0, $9) to (320, $21), parallel to MPC. No dots, projection guides or brackets are drawn.

medium.q: Which change in incentives would move the fast-fashion garments market toward its socially efficient quantity?
options: Raise the private marginal cost faced by producers
Lower the marginal cost faced by producers
Shift MPB upward by the external cost
Set output at the unregulated market quantity
medium.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
medium.feedback: The tax makes producers face the $6 marginal external cost, aligning private marginal cost with MSC and moving quantity to 160 million garments.
medium.imageAlt: Graph of fast-fashion garments (millions) with labeled marginal curves.
medium.graphDescription: The horizontal axis measures fast-fashion garments (millions), from 0 to 320. The vertical axis measures marginal benefit and cost in dollars per garment. MPB is a straight line from (0, $21) to (320, $9). MPC is a straight line from (0, $3) to (320, $15). MSC is a straight line from (0, $9) to (320, $21), parallel to MPC. No dots, projection guides or brackets are drawn.

medium.q: If no corrective policy is adopted, how will the market quantity of disposable vapes compare with the socially efficient quantity?
options: The market underconsumes by 40 thousand vapes
The market is efficient at 180 thousand vapes
The market overconsumes by 140 thousand vapes
The market overconsumes by 40 thousand vapes

medium.q: What distinguishes an external cost from an ordinary private cost?
options: It is always paid as a tax
It is any expense a seller records
An external cost falls on a third party outside the transaction
It exists only for public goods
medium.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
medium.feedback: External effects reach people outside the exchange. Costs already paid by the buyer or seller are private; an external cost is omitted from their exchange and therefore from the market price.

medium.q: Why does the sign of an externality not reveal its production or consumption channel?
options: Sign and channel are always the same
Only production creates positive spillovers
Only consumption creates negative spillovers
Sign identifies harm or benefit; channel identifies which activity creates it
medium.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
medium.feedback: Sign and source are separate dimensions. A positive or negative sign identifies the effect on third parties, whereas production or consumption identifies the activity that generates it.

medium.q: A firm's research helps other firms imitate a process. Which private-social relationship is likely?
options: Social benefit of production exceeds the producer's private benefit
Social cost of consumption exceeds private cost
Private benefit of consumption exceeds social benefit
The effect is negative because rivals benefit
medium.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
medium.feedback: Knowledge spillovers can make social production returns exceed private returns. Because imitators receive gains without compensating the innovator, private production incentives can be weaker than the total social return.

medium.q: Buyers receive all benefits and sellers bear all costs of a trade. What externality evidence is present?
options: A negative production externality
None from those facts alone
A positive consumption externality
Both positive and negative externalities
medium.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
medium.feedback: An externality requires a third-party effect. Benefits and costs confined to the transacting parties are already private; evidence of a spillover requires an effect on someone else.

medium.q: A factory ignores a constant marginal pollution cost. Relative to efficient quantity, what does the market tend to produce?
options: Too little output
The efficient output automatically
Too much output
Zero output in every case
medium.commonError: Using private curves alone when social costs or benefits determine efficiency.
medium.feedback: Ignoring external cost makes private marginal cost too low. The factory compares MPB with MPC and omits pollution damage, so MPC lies below MSC and the private intersection occurs at too much output.

medium.q: Consumers ignore harms their purchases impose on bystanders. What is the usual quantity result?
options: Underconsumption
No quantity distortion
A shortage caused by a price ceiling
Overconsumption
medium.commonError: Using private curves alone when social costs or benefits determine efficiency.
medium.feedback: Private marginal benefit exceeds social marginal benefit. When consumers omit harm to bystanders, MPB lies above MSB and the market chooses units whose social benefit is below their social cost.

medium.q: Plants have different abatement costs, but a regulator orders equal cuts. What concern arises?
options: The same aggregate reduction may cost more than necessary
The policy changes a negative externality into a positive one
Equal cuts guarantee equal marginal costs
The rule automatically creates tax revenue
medium.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
medium.feedback: Uniform cuts can ignore marginal-cost differences. Equal cuts ignore differences in marginal abatement cost, so the target could be reached with less total cost by shifting reductions toward lower-cost plants.

medium.q: A safety rule bans disposal of toxic waste in a river. What is its intended mechanism?
options: Subsidize river disposal
Prevent the harmful action rather than price each unit
Create a tradable cap automatically
Guarantee compensation to every resident
medium.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
medium.feedback: A prohibition directly restricts the action. A ban is a direct quantity restriction: it prevents the damaging behavior instead of charging a price for each unit of harm.

medium.q: How does an emissions standard differ from a corrective tax?
options: A standard fixes a legal quantity constraint; a tax sets a price on harm
A standard creates revenue while a tax never does
A tax fixes emissions with certainty
They are identical whenever enforced
medium.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
medium.feedback: Quantity and price instruments use different control variables. A standard determines an allowed quantity, while a corrective tax changes the marginal private price; those instruments need not produce identical certainty or revenue.

medium.q: Why might a performance standard be preferred to mandated technology?
options: It removes monitoring needs
It can let firms choose how to meet the required outcome
It guarantees zero compliance cost
It turns the externality into a public good
medium.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
medium.feedback: Performance standards preserve some compliance flexibility. Firms retain freedom to select the least-cost method, although regulators still must define, monitor, and enforce the performance outcome.

medium.q: A corrective tax equals marginal external cost at efficient output. What does it accomplish?
options: It makes the decision-maker face the omitted social cost
It guarantees sellers bear the legal tax
It eliminates distributional effects
It makes revenue equal DWL
medium.commonError: Confusing the corrective wedge, incidence, revenue, and deadweight loss.
medium.feedback: The tax internalizes marginal external cost. At the efficient quantity, adding the tax to the private margin closes the gap between private and social cost and removes the incentive to choose harmful excess units.

medium.q: Why is tax revenue not the same as deadweight loss?
options: Revenue is always larger than social costs
Revenue is a transfer; deadweight loss is forgone net social surplus
Deadweight loss is a producer transfer
They are identical with downward demand
medium.commonError: Confusing the corrective wedge, incidence, revenue, and deadweight loss.
medium.feedback: Transfers and efficiency losses differ. Tax revenue changes who holds purchasing power, while deadweight loss measures mutually beneficial surplus that disappears because quantity is inefficient.

medium.q: Why can a positive production externality make output too low?
options: MPC exceeds every buyer's willingness to pay
Producers do not receive the full social benefit they create
Consumers impose an external cost
MSC is always above MPC
medium.commonError: Reversing social and private curves or predicting overproduction instead of underproduction.
medium.feedback: Omitted external benefits weaken private incentives. For a positive production externality, MSC lies below MPC because some production benefit reaches third parties rather than the producer.

medium.q: Why is subsidy expenditure not proof that a positive-externality policy raises welfare?
options: Every subsidy is equal DWL
Spending determines externality sign
A subsidy cannot change quantity
Correction benefits must be compared with resource and financing costs
medium.commonError: Confusing subsidy expenditure with external benefit or taxing a positive externality.
medium.feedback: Fiscal cost and net social benefit are distinct. Government spending is a fiscal cost, not a direct measure of welfare; policy evaluation must compare the external benefit gained with real resource and financing costs.

medium.q: A regulator issues permits covering exactly 1,000 tons. What fixes aggregate emissions?
options: The total number of valid permits
The number of firms trading
Initial market shares
Tax revenue from trades
medium.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
medium.feedback: The permit total fixes the cap. Each permit authorizes a unit of emissions, so the number of valid permits fixes total legal emissions even when ownership changes through trade.

medium.q: Firm A abates for $20 per ton and B for $70. At a $45 permit price, what is efficient?
options: B abates more because its cost is higher
A abates more and can sell permits; B buys permits and abates less
Both must abate equally
Trading loosens the cap
medium.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
medium.feedback: The lower-cost reducer abates when cost is below permit price. Firm A's $20 abatement cost is below the $45 permit price, while Firm B's $70 cost is above it, so trade assigns more reduction to the lower-cost source.

medium.q: What happens to the emissions cap when two firms trade an existing permit?
options: It rises by one unit
It falls by one unit
The cap is unchanged
It becomes voluntary
medium.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
medium.feedback: Trading reallocates an existing right. A trade transfers permission to emit from one firm to another; it neither creates nor retires a permit and therefore leaves aggregate emissions unchanged.

medium.q: A paper mill buys downstream fishing rights and cuts pollution because it bears lost fishery value. What is illustrated?
options: Business integration internalizes the spillover
A binding price ceiling
A government permit cap
Guaranteed correction through norms
medium.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
medium.feedback: Common ownership brings the external cost into private calculation. Combining ownership makes the mill bear both production gains and fishery losses, bringing a previously external cost into the same private decision.

medium.q: Which feature makes national defense a public good?
options: It is sold by one private firm.
Its marginal cost is always zero.
Consumers can be excluded easily.
It is broadly nonrival and difficult to exclude nonpayers.
medium.commonError: Confusing government provision with the economic definition of a public good.
medium.feedback: Public goods are characterized by nonrivalry and nonexcludability.

medium.q: Why may a privately funded flood barrier receive too little support?
options: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
People can benefit without paying
It is rival with fully enforceable private access
It is a private good supplied by government
medium.commonError: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
medium.feedback: Because households can receive protection without contributing, each has an incentive to free ride, weakening private funding and causing underprovision.

Marginal social benefit
Average fixed cost
The permit price for a common resource

Those added miles have marginal social benefit above marginal cost
The change moves provision toward the efficient intersection
The change makes the project excludable
medium.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.

It becomes private benefit rather than social benefit

The two individual quantities add to MC

medium.q: A town adds electronic gates to an uncongested road that had been open to everyone. Which economic characteristic changes most directly?
options: The road becomes excludable because access can be denied
The road becomes rival even without congestion
The road becomes a public good because government owns it
The road loses scarcity because a toll is charged
medium.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
medium.feedback: Electronic gates make exclusion feasible. The uncongested road can remain nonrival over the stated range, changing its classification from a public-good setting toward a club good.

medium.q: A ticket admits one person to a specific concert seat. Under those conditions, what kind of good is the seat?
options: Private good
Public good
Common resource
Club good
medium.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
medium.feedback: The venue can exclude people without tickets, and assigning the seat to one person leaves it unavailable to another, making it excludable and rival.

medium.q: A streaming service blocks nonmembers, and the platform has ample capacity so one more viewer does not degrade service. What is it?
options: Public good
Private good
Club good
Common resource
medium.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
medium.feedback: The subscription makes access excludable, while spare capacity makes another viewer nonrival over the stated range.

medium.q: An uncongested express lane requires an electronic toll. How should access to the lane be classified?
options: Club good
Public good
Private good
Common resource
medium.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
medium.feedback: The toll makes the lane excludable, and with no congestion an additional driver does not reduce service quality for others, so it is nonrival over that range.

medium.q: A citywide mosquito-control program benefits properties throughout the treated area, including nonpayers, without reducing protection for others. Which category fits?
options: Private good
Common resource
Club good
Public good
medium.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
medium.feedback: Area-wide mosquito control is nonexcludable under the stated delivery method and nonrival because one household's benefit does not reduce another's.

medium.q: Farmers can pump from an unregulated shared aquifer, and each withdrawal lowers the water available to others. Which category fits?
options: Public good
Private good
Common resource
Club good
medium.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
medium.feedback: Access is difficult to exclude and groundwater withdrawals are rival because they reduce the shared stock.

medium.q: A downtown road has no toll and is heavily congested. What category best describes road space at that time?
options: Common resource
Public good
Private good
Club good
medium.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
medium.feedback: Access is nonexcludable without a toll or gate, and congestion makes road space rival because each driver adds delay for others.

medium.q: A fenced timber parcel has an enforceable owner, and trees harvested by one buyer cannot be harvested by another. How is the timber classified?
options: Public good
Common resource
Private good
Club good
medium.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
medium.feedback: Enforced ownership permits exclusion and harvesting depletes the available timber, making it rival.

medium.q: An unencrypted radio signal reaches every receiver in its broadcast area. Why is it nonexcludable?
options: Listening uses up the signal
The station faces no production cost
The station cannot feasibly block individual nonpayers from receiving it
Government owns every receiver
medium.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
medium.feedback: With an open broadcast, individual nonpayers cannot feasibly be denied reception, which makes consumption nonexcludable.

medium.q: A private park requires a membership card at its only entrance. Which conclusion follows?
options: The park is nonexcludable because nature is shared
The park is excludable because nonmembers can be turned away
The park is rival only because it charges
The park must be a private good even when empty
medium.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
medium.feedback: A controlled entrance makes denial of access feasible. Excludability alone does not determine rivalry or the final four-way classification.

medium.q: A news site removes its paywall and permits unlimited anonymous reading. Which dimension changes?
options: It becomes more rival
It becomes legally prohibited
It becomes a common resource because information is depleted
It becomes less excludable
medium.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
medium.feedback: Removing the paywall makes it difficult to deny content to nonpayers; it does not make digital information rival.

medium.q: A city posts hurricane maps online without login restrictions. Which statement about consumption is correct?
options: The maps are rival because many people download them
The maps are nonexcludable under the stated access policy
The maps are excludable because the city created them
The maps are private goods because servers cost money
medium.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
medium.feedback: Open access means users cannot be denied based on payment. Production cost and public ownership do not determine excludability.

medium.q: A government service is available only to users who present a paid permit. Which inference is valid?
options: The service can be excludable even though government provides it
Government provision makes every service nonexcludable
The permit makes consumption nonrival
The service must be a common resource
medium.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
medium.feedback: Who supplies a good does not determine its economic category. A paid permit can make access excludable.

medium.q: Thousands of households receive the same uncrowded radio signal. Why is reception nonrival?
options: Another listener does not reduce the signal available to others
The station can charge every listener
Stations do not compete
Broadcast equipment has no cost
medium.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
medium.feedback: Nonrivalry means adding a listener does not diminish the signal or reception available to existing listeners.

medium.q: An extra download of a digital report does not slow the server or delete anyone's copy. Which characteristic is present?
options: Nonexcludability
Rivalry among publishers
Nonrivalry
Resource depletion
medium.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
medium.feedback: The extra download leaves the report fully available to others, so consumption is nonrival under the stated capacity conditions.

medium.q: A toll road is uncongested at midnight. Which statement about rivalry is most accurate?
options: One more car may be nonrival because it does not slow other drivers
The toll makes every trip rival
Road ownership determines rivalry
The road must be a common resource
medium.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
medium.feedback: The toll determines exclusion. With ample capacity, an additional car does not reduce service quality, so use can be nonrival over that range.

medium.q: Which statement correctly separates rivalry from firm competition?
options: Rivalry counts the number of sellers
Rivalry asks whether a good is legal
Rivalry is another name for excludability
Rivalry asks whether one person's use reduces what others can consume
medium.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
medium.feedback: Consumption rivalry concerns depletion or congestion, not the competitive structure of the supplying industry.

medium.q: Why can observed donations understate demand for a pure public good?
options: Public goods have no social benefit
Donations always exceed marginal cost
Rival consumption forces people to donate twice
Noncontributors may still benefit, weakening incentives to reveal willingness to pay
medium.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
medium.feedback: Voluntary payments reveal only contributed private willingness to pay. Free riders can enjoy the good while withholding part of their valuation.

medium.q: How can free riding lead to too little mosquito control?
options: Each treated household uses up the protection
Voluntary contributions can fall below the total social willingness to pay
Private payments necessarily exceed MSB
Mosquito control becomes a common resource
medium.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
medium.feedback: Area-wide treatment benefits noncontributors, so private contributions may not capture all social benefit and provision can stop below the efficient level.

medium.q: A public safety website is funded by voluntary gifts. Many users assume enough other people will donate. What is the likely result?
options: The website becomes rival
Every user reveals full willingness to pay
The efficient quantity must be zero
Contributions may be too low relative to the site's social benefit
medium.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
medium.feedback: When each user relies on others to fund a nonexcludable service, aggregate contributions can be insufficient even when users collectively value it highly.

medium.q: If exclusion technology becomes effective for a formerly open broadcast, what happens to the free-rider problem?
options: It intensifies because payment becomes easier
It is unchanged because excludability never matters
It can weaken because access can be conditioned on payment
It turns automatically into common-resource overuse
medium.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
medium.feedback: When nonpayers can be denied access, receiving the benefit depends more directly on payment, reducing the incentive to free ride.

medium.q: Which observation would be strongest evidence of free riding in a clean-air alert service?
options: Contributors receive email receipts
Many noncontributors regularly use the alerts
The service has a positive operating cost
Two firms offer weather forecasts
medium.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
medium.feedback: Use by noncontributors shows people obtaining the nonexcludable benefit without helping finance it.

medium.q: For a pure public good with no exclusion or alternative revenue, why may a profit-seeking firm provide too little?
options: It cannot collect payment from everyone who benefits
Its marginal cost must be zero
Every customer consumes a different quantity
Public goods cannot be produced with labor
medium.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
medium.feedback: Nonexcludability makes it difficult to charge all beneficiaries, so revenue reflects less than the good's total social benefit.

medium.q: A company funds free weather alerts with advertising. Why can provision occur despite open access?
options: Advertising makes the alerts rival
Open access guarantees subscription fees
Advertisers provide an alternative source of revenue
The company no longer faces costs
medium.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
medium.feedback: The firm need not charge each listener when advertisers pay for access to the audience, partially solving the direct-payment problem.

medium.q: A business association signs a contract to finance district-wide security patrols. What problem does the contract address?
options: It makes patrols rival
It coordinates payment for a benefit that reaches many businesses
It guarantees zero enforcement cost
It removes every nonmember from the district
medium.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
medium.feedback: A binding contract can collect coordinated payments and reduce reliance on unilateral voluntary contributions.

medium.q: Why can a subscription convert some information services into club goods?
options: Access controls make nonpayment grounds for exclusion
Information becomes physically depleted
Subscriptions eliminate marginal cost
Subscribers stop sharing a common quantity
medium.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
medium.feedback: A subscription lets the provider deny access to nonmembers, making revenue collection feasible while consumption can remain nonrival over the relevant range.

medium.q: How can free riding bias a survey used to value a proposed public good?
options: Respondents must overstate marginal cost
The survey makes the good rival
Only nonbeneficiaries answer surveys
Respondents may understate willingness to pay if answers affect their expected contribution
medium.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
medium.feedback: People who expect to receive the good regardless of payment may report low values to reduce their expected cost share.

medium.q: Why might voluntary donations be a poor measure of total benefit from a public warning system?
options: Donations include only marginal cost
Noncontributors can benefit, so donations omit part of willingness to pay
Warning systems are rival
Total benefit equals government spending
medium.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
medium.feedback: Observed gifts reflect contributed private payments, not necessarily the full value received by contributors and free riders.

medium.q: Why do boats tend to catch too many fish in an open-access fishery?
options: Each boat receives the catch benefit but shares the depletion cost with all users
Fish are nonrival
Each boat pays the full opportunity cost imposed on others
Open access guarantees conservation
medium.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
medium.feedback: A boat captures much of its private gain while imposing part of the reduced future stock on other boats, so private incentives favor excessive harvest.

medium.q: On open grazing land, why might each herder add another animal even when total grazing is excessive?
options: Forage is nonrival
The herder bears every depletion cost
Adding animals makes the land excludable
The herder gets the added animal's benefit while spreading pasture damage across all herders
medium.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
medium.feedback: Private benefit is concentrated, while reduced forage and land damage are shared, so individual incentives can produce collective overgrazing.

medium.q: Why is the tragedy of the commons an incentive problem rather than merely selfish behavior?
options: Common resources have no value
Open access separates private gains from part of the social depletion cost
All users prefer destroying the resource
Rivalry eliminates scarcity
medium.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
medium.feedback: Even ordinary users face an incentive to take the private benefit now because much of the depletion cost falls on the group.

medium.q: Which outcome distinguishes common-resource overuse from public-good underprovision?
options: Both necessarily have insufficient use
Both are excludable and rival
Public goods are depleted while common resources are not
Common resources tend toward excessive use, while public goods tend toward insufficient provision
medium.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
medium.feedback: Nonexcludable public goods invite free riding on payment and underprovision; rival common resources invite use without full depletion cost and overuse.

medium.q: Why can an individual fisher's private marginal cost be below the social marginal cost of a catch?
options: Fish are a public good
The fisher does not bear the full reduction in future catch opportunities for others
The fisher pays every stock cost immediately
Social cost excludes depletion
medium.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
medium.feedback: The private calculation omits part of the opportunity cost imposed on other users through a smaller future stock.

medium.q: A market has one dominant seller that can influence price. Why might the market outcome be inefficient?

Opportunity cost no longer applies
The dominant seller must produce the efficient quantity.
medium.commonError: thinks_market_power_only_means_large_firm_not_distortion
medium.feedback: Market power can allow a seller to influence price and reduce market efficiency.

medium.q: A dominant platform blocks entry and reduces trades. What is the core concern?
options: Blocking entry makes the platform nonexcludable
Reducing trades creates a public-good free-rider problem
The platform’s size by itself proves a negative externality.
Market power can keep quantity below the efficient level
medium.commonError: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
medium.feedback: Market power can restrict mutually beneficial trades by influencing price or quantity.

hard.q: At the next unit of a competitive product, a buyer values it at $18, the producer uses $14 of resources, and pollution harms neighbors by $6. Which outcome does a $6 per-unit tax encourage?
options: Forgo the unit: private gains are $4 but net social benefit is -$2.
Produce the unit: the $4 private gain measures its full social benefit.
Produce the unit: $6 of tax revenue makes its net social benefit $4.
Forgo the unit: every taxed unit has zero social benefit.
hard.commonError: Treating a corrective tax as unrelated to marginal incentives.
hard.feedback: The trade has a private gain of 18 - 14 = $4, but net social benefit is 18 - 14 - 6 = -$2. A $6 tax makes the relevant private cost $20, above willingness to pay. Revenue is a transfer, not an extra resource benefit.
