legendary.q: Two systems reach the same cap; one allocates permits equally and one auctions them. What must be separated?
options: Aggregate emissions from trading
Cost-effective emissions allocation from distribution of permit value
External cost from private cost
The cap from permit count
legendary.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
legendary.feedback: Allocation can change wealth without changing the least-cost emissions allocation. Both systems can reach the same least-cost allocation through trading, while the initial distribution or auction of permits changes who receives the scarcity rents.

legendary.q: Plants would emit 500 tons without abatement. A binding cap is reduced to 420 tons. The first 50 tons can be abated for $10 each; the next 50 for $30 each, with no other abatement or trading costs. What allocation and total cost meet the new cap most cheaply?
options: Abate 80 low-cost tons for $800, even though only 50 are available.
Abate 40 tons in each cost group for $1,600.
Abate 420 tons because the new cap is the required reduction.
Abate all 50 low-cost tons and 30 higher-cost tons, for $1,400.
legendary.commonError: Assuming permit allocation changes the cap or that all firms should abate equally.
legendary.feedback: Required abatement is 500 - 420 = 80 tons. Exhaust the 50 tons at $10, then use 30 at $30: 500 + 900 = $1,400. The cap limits remaining emissions, while trading can allocate reductions to the cheaper opportunities.

legendary.q: A landlord can insulate a noisy building for $700. The improvement raises the present value of rents by $500 and gives neighboring properties $400 of additional benefits. There are no other effects. Neighbors could organize a payment at a real cost of $250. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: The landlord installs without a payment because all $900 of benefits become its rent.
The proposed bargain creates $200 of net gains because coordination costs are transfers.
Insulation is socially wasteful because benefits outside the building do not count.
Insulation is socially worthwhile before coordination costs, but neither rent capture alone nor that bargain finances it with positive joint gains.
legendary.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
legendary.feedback: Total benefit is 500 + 400 = $900, above the $700 cost by $200. The landlord captures only $500. Coordinating neighbors consumes $250, more than the available $200 joint gain, so that arrangement does not close the incentive gap profitably.

legendary.q: Thousands of dispersed residents each suffer a small pollution loss. Why may negotiation fail?
options: Organizing and bargaining costs can exceed gains
Harm becomes private benefit
Large numbers guarantee compensation
Rights cease to affect distribution
legendary.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
legendary.feedback: Large groups can make coordination too costly. When many parties each have small stakes, locating participants, coordinating terms, preventing holdouts, and enforcing payment can consume the bargaining surplus.

legendary.q: A polluter has the right to continue operating. Option A prevents $900 of damage, costs $500 to install and $100 to contract. Option B prevents $1,200 of damage, costs $650 to install and $300 to contract. Victims pay all contract costs; transfers have no resource cost. Which option offers the larger bargaining surplus, and what payment interval supports it?
options: Option B: more than $650 but less than $900, because it prevents more damage.
Option A: more than $500 but less than $800 paid to the polluter.
Option A: more than $500 but less than $900, because contracting uses no resources.
Option B: exactly $1,200, because all avoided damage must become compensation.
legendary.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
legendary.feedback: A yields 900 - 500 - 100 = $300; B yields 1200 - 650 - 300 = $250. Under A, a payment above $500 covers the polluter’s cost, while one below $800 leaves victims better off after their $100 contracting cost.

legendary.q: A contract creates $1,200 in joint gains but costs $350 to negotiate and enforce. What net gain remains?
legendary.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
legendary.feedback: Net gain is $1,200 - $350. Negotiation and enforcement costs use $350 of the $1,200 gross surplus, leaving $850 available to make the parties better off.

legendary.q: Noise reduction costs $700 and benefits neighbors $1,000. Agreement costs $400. Is bargaining worthwhile?
options: Yes; every external benefit guarantees bargaining
Yes; net gain is $700
No; initial rights prevent efficiency
No; the $300 gross gain is below the $400 transaction cost
legendary.commonError: Assuming any voluntary response necessarily eliminates the entire externality.
legendary.feedback: Gross gain is $300, below transaction cost. The action creates only $300 of gross joint surplus, so spending $400 to reach and enforce an agreement would make the bargain inefficient.

legendary.q: Preventing a spillover avoids $2 million of harm and uses $1.2 million of resources. A bargain adds $1 million in real transaction costs. An enforceable regulation can achieve the same prevention with $0.3 million of administration and compliance costs beyond prevention. With no other effects, which ranking follows?
options: The bargain gains $0.8 million and ranks first because transfers are voluntary.
No prevention ranks first because failed bargaining proves prevention is inefficient.
Regulation loses $0.7 million because avoided harm should be excluded from policy evaluation.
Regulation gains $0.5 million; no prevention ranks next; the bargain loses $0.2 million.
legendary.commonError: Treating Coase bargaining as costless or as proof that initial rights never matter.
legendary.feedback: Gross prevention gains are 2 - 1.2 = $0.8 million. Net gains are 0.8 - 1 = -$0.2 million for this bargain and 0.8 - 0.3 = $0.5 million for regulation. Bargaining failure does not establish that every feasible remedy fails.

legendary.q: A fishery is open to many boats, and each boat ignores how its catch reduces future stocks for others. Which policy logic fits?
options: Subsidize every additional catch.
Limit or price access so users face more of the depletion cost.
Remove all information about stocks.
Set a price ceiling on fish without limiting harvest.
legendary.commonError: Choosing a policy that strengthens overuse incentives.
legendary.feedback: Access rules, quotas, or charges can internalize the shared depletion cost.

legendary.q: A navigation app is nonrival after creation but can exclude unpaid users. What is the best conclusion?
options: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
It is a private good supplied by government
It is nonrival but easy to exclude
It is not a pure public good because exclusion is feasible
legendary.commonError: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
legendary.feedback: The app is nonrival but excludable, so it is not a pure public good; it is closer to a club good.

legendary.q: A fishery uses quotas, but regulators cannot observe illegal catch. What complicates the remedy?
options: Enforcement and information constraints affect performance
Any intervention is automatically costless
Identifying failure proves one remedy is optimal
Administrative incentives and information do not matter
legendary.commonError: Treating identified failure as proof that any intervention is superior.
legendary.feedback: Compare feasible responses, administrative costs, information limits, and unintended effects.

legendary.q: An open-access aquifer is depleted. What private-social divergence occurs?
options: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
It is rival with fully enforceable private access
Each user ignores depletion costs shared by others
It is a private good supplied by government
legendary.commonError: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
legendary.feedback: Each user receives the private benefit of pumping water but bears only part of the depletion cost imposed on other users, creating an incentive to overuse the aquifer.

legendary.q: A town hires contractors to supply rival packed meals, an uncrowded archive behind a login, and an unencrypted nonrival warning broadcast. It proposes charging for each meal, opening the archive after securing full sponsorship, and coordinating payment for the warning through a binding community agreement. Which assessment links the goods characteristics to those funding choices?
options: Private contractors make all three goods rival, so each additional user must be rationed through an individual charge.
Opening the archive turns it into a depleted common resource, while collecting warning contributions makes warning reception excludable.
Meals still require allocation among rival users; sponsorship can finance open nonrival access; the agreement can address warning-service free riding.
Meal fees solve the warning’s free-rider problem automatically, so the community agreement cannot change provision.
legendary.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
legendary.feedback: Meal consumption uses up a rival unit. Archive exclusion can change without creating rivalry, and sponsorship can replace login revenue. The warning remains nonexcludable, but a binding funding agreement can coordinate contributions. Consumption characteristics and financing institutions must be evaluated separately.

legendary.q: A freely broadcast emergency alert reaches every receiver in range and one listener does not weaken the signal for another. What is it?
options: Public good
Private good
Common resource
Club good
legendary.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
legendary.feedback: The open signal is difficult to exclude and nonrival in reception, satisfying both public-good dimensions.

legendary.q: A digital hazard map is initially open, nonrival and free to copy. Verified accounts can enforce a paywall at a real cost. A paywall would finance updates but exclude some users whose benefit exceeds the near-zero cost of serving them. Which evaluation is complete?
options: Adopt the paywall whenever revenue increases, because all lost access represents wasted consumption.
Reject account verification because nonrival information cannot be made excludable.
Treat account enforcement as a change in rivalry rather than a change in feasible exclusion.
Compare the benefit of financed updates with exclusion losses and enforcement costs; better revenue does not alone prove higher welfare.
legendary.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
legendary.feedback: Technology can make a nonrival service excludable and improve revenue capture. That can support useful updates while also blocking valuable low-cost access and consuming enforcement resources. Net welfare depends on all three effects.

legendary.q: A password is shared widely and the provider cannot identify unauthorized users. What limits effective excludability?
options: Authorized use becomes rival automatically
The access rule is difficult to enforce
The service has no marginal cost
The provider is privately owned
legendary.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
legendary.feedback: A nominal password rule does not create strong exclusion when unauthorized use cannot be detected or stopped.

legendary.q: A nonexcludable siren project is worth $300 to each of five households and costs $1,000. One household cannot finance it alone. A binding agreement would collect $200 from each household only if all five sign, with no contracting costs. Which comparison follows?
options: The project is inefficient because no single household values it at its full $1,000 cost.
Uncoordinated funding can fail despite $500 of total gains; the conditional agreement can make every household $100 better off.
The agreement makes the siren rival because every household now pays a fee.
The agreement creates $1,000 of new social benefit solely by collecting contributions.
legendary.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
legendary.feedback: Total value is 5 x 300 = $1,500, leaving $500 after resource cost. Each household gains 300 - 200 = $100 under the binding agreement. It coordinates contributions without changing the warning’s rivalry or excludability.

legendary.q: A neighborhood patrol benefits every home on a block, including households that decline the fee. What is the central financing problem?
options: Protection is consumed by the first household
Fees make the patrol nonrival
The patrol creates open-access depletion
Each household may wait for others to pay for the shared protection
legendary.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
legendary.feedback: The patrol's nonexcludable benefit gives households an incentive to enjoy protection financed by their neighbors.

legendary.q: A nonrival safety bulletin yields $1,500 of total user benefit when open and costs $900 to produce. Donations provide $500. A sponsor would pay $1,000 to keep it open; alternatively, a paywall yields $1,100 of receipts, retains $1,200 of user benefit and costs $100 to enforce. Treat payments as transfers and assume no other effects. Which financing plan is viable and gives larger net social benefit?
options: The paywall: its $1,100 receipts prove greater welfare than the sponsor’s $1,000 payment.
Donations: $1,500 of benefit means the producer can cover costs with $500 of receipts.
Sponsorship: it covers production and preserves $600 of net social benefit, versus $200 under the paywall.
Both paid plans yield identical welfare because information remains nonrival.
legendary.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
legendary.feedback: Sponsorship receipts cover $900 of cost and leave net social benefit 1500 - 900 = $600. Paywall receipts cover production plus enforcement, but net social benefit is 1200 - 900 - 100 = $200. Revenue feasibility and welfare are separate comparisons.

legendary.q: A village’s open fishery is depleted while its nonexcludable flood-warning system receives too few contributions. Leaders propose a catch fee and a collective warning-service fund. Which diagnosis explains why the two remedies target different margins?
options: Both remedies should discourage consumption because fish and warnings are depleted by each user.
The fee discourages rival extraction that harms other users; the fund coordinates payment for a shared nonrival benefit.
Both remedies should subsidize individual use because nonexcludability always causes too little consumption.
The fishery needs only voluntary donations, while the warning requires a catch-style quantity quota.
legendary.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
legendary.feedback: The fishery combines difficult exclusion with rival use, encouraging excessive extraction. The warning is nonrival and nonexcludable, encouraging underpayment and underprovision. Similar access problems need different incentives because rivalry differs.

legendary.q: A broadband network has high fixed cost and low marginal cost. Marginal-cost pricing would expand valuable access but leave a financing deficit. Average-cost pricing can cover costs but excludes some users whose value exceeds marginal cost. Public support has a real collection cost. What information is needed to choose between the two rules?
options: Only whether marginal-cost pricing creates an accounting loss, because loss proves social inefficiency.
Only whether average-cost pricing breaks even, because break-even proves maximum social surplus.
The extra access benefits net of resource cost, compared with the real cost of financing the deficit.
Only the subsidy payment, because every transferred dollar is a destroyed social resource.
legendary.commonError: Ignoring the pricing and cost-recovery tradeoff.
legendary.feedback: The financing problem and the access distortion are distinct. Compare additional gains from valuable access with financing’s real costs under feasible support arrangements. Accounting losses and transfer amounts do not alone rank the rules.

legendary.q: An exclusive right lets an innovator charge above marginal cost. Removing it would expand current access but could reduce future investment in similar products. Which evidence is needed before claiming removal raises welfare?
options: Only the current markup, because all markups equal net profit and total social loss.
Only the innovator’s revenue, because consumer gains are transfers that cannot affect welfare.
Only the number of new buyers, because future incentives are unrelated to exclusive rights.
Gains from additional current trades and the size of any resulting loss of valuable future innovation.
legendary.commonError: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
legendary.feedback: Market power can exclude mutually beneficial current purchases, while expected returns can affect investment. A welfare comparison needs both margins and cannot be settled by the markup or seller revenue alone. This asks about incentives, not a legal test.

easyBoss.q: A factory pollutes a river used by nearby residents. What kind of market failure is this?
options: A negative externality
A public good
A price floor
A positive externality.
easyBoss.feedback: Pollution harms bystanders who are not part of the transaction, so it is a negative externality.

easyBoss.q: Refer to the emergency-sirens graph. At what quantity do MSB and MC intersect?
options: 40 sirens
20 sirens
30 sirens
60 sirens
easyBoss.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
easyBoss.feedback: MSB intersects MC at 40 sirens, so the marginal social benefit of the 40th siren equals its marginal cost.
easyBoss.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.
easyBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

easyBoss.q: Refer to the graph. Why is 40, rather than the largest displayed quantity, the efficient number of sirens?
options: The 40th siren is the point where MSB equals MC
Every resident buys exactly one siren at 40
Total benefit becomes zero at 40
Marginal cost is minimized only at 40
easyBoss.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
easyBoss.feedback: The graph places the MSB-MC intersection at 40 sirens. Beyond that point, an additional siren's cost exceeds its added social benefit even though total benefit remains positive.
easyBoss.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.
easyBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

easyBoss.q: In the local-public-radio graph, where does the Private Benefit curve intersect MC?
options: 20 hours per week
60 hours per week
40 hours per week
80 hours per week
easyBoss.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
easyBoss.feedback: Private Benefit equals MC at 40 hours, identifying the quantity supported by the revealed private incentive in this pure-public-good setting.
easyBoss.imageAlt: Local public radio graph: Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours and MSB intersects MC at 80 hours per week.
easyBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is hours of local public radio programming per week. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in hundreds of dollars per hour. MSB equals 100 minus Q, Private Benefit equals 60 minus Q, and MC equals 20. Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours; MSB intersects MC at 80 hours.

easyBoss.q: Refer to the graph. At 40 hours of local public radio, what is MSB?
options: $2,000 per hour
$4,000 per hour
$6,000 per hour
$8,000 per hour
easyBoss.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
easyBoss.feedback: At Q = 40, the graph shows MSB at 60 on an axis measured in hundreds of dollars per hour, so marginal social benefit is $6,000 per hour. MC is $2,000 per hour.
easyBoss.imageAlt: Local public radio graph: Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours and MSB intersects MC at 80 hours per week.
easyBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is hours of local public radio programming per week. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in hundreds of dollars per hour. MSB equals 100 minus Q, Private Benefit equals 60 minus Q, and MC equals 20. Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours; MSB intersects MC at 80 hours.

mediumBoss.q: Which case is a negative externality?
options: Noise from a venue reducing nearby residents’ well-being.
A buyer paying the posted price.
A student receiving private tutoring that affects only the student and tutor.
A firm lowering its own cost.
mediumBoss.commonError: Misidentifying the source of market failure.
mediumBoss.feedback: Noise that reduces nearby residents’ well-being imposes a cost on third parties outside the transaction, so it is a negative externality.

mediumBoss.q: Why might a public good be underprovided privately?
options: Use by one person prevents all others from using it.
People can benefit without paying, weakening voluntary funding.
Exclusion is effortless.
Every consumer reveals exact willingness to pay.
mediumBoss.commonError: Misidentifying the source of market failure.
mediumBoss.feedback: When nonpayers can benefit from the good, individuals have an incentive to free ride, so voluntary private funding can be below the efficient level.

mediumBoss.q: Refer to the graph. At the efficient emergency-siren quantity, what marginal benefit and marginal cost are shown?
options: $10,000 per siren
$20,000 per siren
$30,000 per siren
$40,000 per siren
mediumBoss.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
mediumBoss.feedback: At 40 sirens, the graph shows 20 on an axis measured in thousands of dollars per siren, so MSB and MC both equal $20,000 per siren.
mediumBoss.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.
mediumBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

mediumBoss.q: If 50 emergency sirens have been installed, which marginal comparison follows from the graph?
options: MSB exceeds MC, so the system is underprovided
MSB equals MC, so 50 is efficient
Private Benefit exceeds MSB
MC exceeds MSB, so the last sirens are overprovided
mediumBoss.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
mediumBoss.feedback: At 50 sirens, the graph shows MSB of $15,000 and MC of $20,000. Marginal cost exceeds marginal social benefit, indicating provision beyond the efficient 40 sirens.
mediumBoss.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.
mediumBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

mediumBoss.q: Refer to the graph. At 20 emergency sirens, what value does the MSB curve show?
options: $10,000 per siren
$30,000 per siren
$20,000 per siren
$40,000 per siren
mediumBoss.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
mediumBoss.feedback: At Q = 20, the MSB curve is at 30 on an axis measured in thousands of dollars per siren, so marginal social benefit is $30,000 per siren.
mediumBoss.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.
mediumBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

mediumBoss.q: The siren system warns all residents at once and an additional listener does not reduce the warning available to others. Which feature does that illustrate?
options: Nonrivalry in consumption
Rivalry among suppliers
Excludability through pricing
Depletion of a common resource
mediumBoss.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
mediumBoss.feedback: The warning reaches additional residents without reducing the warning available to anyone else, so consumption is nonrival under the stated conditions.

mediumBoss.q: What is the standard efficiency concern with market power?
options: Every firm earns zero accounting profit.
All prices fall below marginal cost.
Output may be restricted below the level where buyer value exceeds production cost.
Products become nonrival when one firm sets the market price.
mediumBoss.commonError: Misidentifying the source of market failure.
mediumBoss.feedback: Market power can restrict output below the efficient quantity, leaving mutually beneficial trades unrealized and creating deadweight loss.

finalBoss.q: Suppose the community currently has 30 emergency sirens. What does the graph imply about one more siren?
options: Its marginal cost exceeds its marginal social benefit
Its marginal social benefit is zero
Its marginal social benefit exceeds its marginal cost
Its provision cannot affect net social benefit
finalBoss.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
finalBoss.feedback: At 30 sirens, the graph shows MSB of $25,000 and MC of $20,000. Another siren adds more social benefit than cost, so expanding provision raises net social benefit.
finalBoss.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.
finalBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

finalBoss.q: Which statement best describes the MC curve in the emergency-sirens graph?
options: Total siren cost is fixed at $20,000
Marginal cost falls by $500 per siren
Only the first siren has a cost
Each additional siren costs $20,000 over the shown range
finalBoss.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
finalBoss.feedback: The horizontal MC curve is at 20 on an axis measured in thousands of dollars per siren, so each additional siren costs $20,000; total cost is not fixed.
finalBoss.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.
finalBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

finalBoss.q: Based on the two intersections shown in the graph, how much lower is private provision than efficient provision?
options: 40 hours per week
20 hours per week
60 hours per week
80 hours per week
finalBoss.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
finalBoss.feedback: Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours while MSB intersects MC at 80 hours. The underprovision gap is 80 - 40 = 40 hours.
finalBoss.imageAlt: Local public radio graph: Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours and MSB intersects MC at 80 hours per week.
finalBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is hours of local public radio programming per week. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in hundreds of dollars per hour. MSB equals 100 minus Q, Private Benefit equals 60 minus Q, and MC equals 20. Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours; MSB intersects MC at 80 hours.

finalBoss.q: For nonexcludable radio programming, which change could let a private organization provide more programming despite free riding?
options: Making the signal more nonexcludable
A sponsorship contract that pays for audience-wide benefits
Ignoring benefits to noncontributors
Assuming every listener voluntarily reveals full willingness to pay
finalBoss.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
finalBoss.feedback: A sponsorship contract supplies an alternative revenue mechanism that can capture some audience-wide benefit even when nonpayers cannot be excluded from the signal.

legendaryBoss.q: A nonrival, nonexcludable water-quality alert system would generate $12,000 in total benefits and cost $8,000 to operate. Individual fee collection would cost $5,000; a binding cooperative funding agreement would cost $1,000. Both could fund the same service. Which evaluation is correct if there are no other effects?
options: Individual collection creates $4,000 of net gains because collection uses no resources.
The cooperative creates $3,000 of net gains; individual collection costs exceed the $4,000 operating surplus.
Both methods create $12,000 of net gains because users benefit whether or not they pay.
Neither can work because a private agreement cannot finance a nonexcludable service.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Before funding costs the gain is 12,000 - 8,000 = $4,000. Net gains are -$1,000 with individual collection and $3,000 with the agreement. Nonexcludability complicates funding but does not rule out every institution.

legendaryBoss.q: A fishery’s paper quota is strict, but hidden catches make actual harvest high. A feasible alternative combines verified landing reports with transferable catch rights. What evidence would establish that this alternative improves net social benefit?
options: The new quota is numerically smaller, regardless of hidden catches or enforcement costs.
Quota holders receive valuable rights, so their transfer income equals the total welfare gain.
Trading occurs frequently, so actual harvest must equal the legally allowed total.
Reduced depletion losses exceed added monitoring and adjustment costs, while transfers permit lower-cost compliance.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treating identified failure as proof that any intervention is superior.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Evaluate actual behavior, not just the announced cap. Verification can reduce hidden harvest; transfers can lower compliance costs. Net improvement requires avoided resource losses to exceed real implementation and adjustment costs.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the sirens graph, treating provision as continuous. A proposal installs 60 rather than the quantity that maximizes net social benefit. What excess provision and loss follow, and can positive total benefits alone justify the proposal?
options: 20 excess sirens and $400,000 of lost net benefit; every dollar spent on them is a net loss.
20 excess sirens and $100,000 of lost net benefit; positive total benefits do not establish that the extra sirens are worthwhile.
40 excess sirens and $200,000 of lost net benefit; the marginal-cost value is the target quantity.
No excess provision; any quantity with positive MSB maximizes net social benefit.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Using observed payments as complete social benefit when willingness to pay is difficult to reveal or measure.
legendaryBoss.feedback: MSB = MC at 40. From 40 to 60, the gap MC - MSB rises from 0 to $10,000 per siren. The excess-loss triangle is 0.5 x 20 x 10,000 = $100,000. Extra sirens may have positive benefit while costing even more.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Emergency warning siren provision graph with downward-sloping MSB and horizontal MC intersecting at 40 sirens and $20,000 per siren.
legendaryBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is the number of emergency warning sirens. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per siren. MSB equals 40 minus 0.5Q and MC equals 20. The curves intersect at 40 sirens, where both equal $20,000 per siren.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the public-radio graph. A fund can raise provision from the quantity supported by Private Benefit to the MSB-MC intersection. It uses $10,000 per week in real administration costs; transfers themselves have no resource cost. Which conclusion is supported?
options: The expansion loses $10,000 because donations already measure the full social marginal benefit.
The expansion gains $150,000 because the entire benefit gap is a rectangle.
The expansion gains $80,000 net because administration is a transfer rather than a resource cost.
The expansion yields $70,000 of net weekly gains; voluntary payments alone omit some beneficiaries’ value.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Private Benefit supports 40 hours; MSB meets MC at 80. The MSB-MC gap falls from $4,000 per hour at 40 to zero at 80. Gross gains are 0.5 x 40 x 4,000 = $80,000; after $10,000 administration they are $70,000.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Local public radio graph: Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours and MSB intersects MC at 80 hours per week.
legendaryBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is hours of local public radio programming per week. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in hundreds of dollars per hour. MSB equals 100 minus Q, Private Benefit equals 60 minus Q, and MC equals 20. Private Benefit intersects MC at 40 hours; MSB intersects MC at 80 hours.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the coastal-protection graph and treat quantity as continuous. A council budgets $700 million to expand from 10 to 30 miles. With no fixed or financing costs, which assessment uses the changing marginal cost correctly?
options: The expansion costs $400 million because its initial marginal cost applies to all 20 miles.
The budget is sufficient: expansion costs $500 million and adds $300 million in net benefits.
The expansion costs $600 million because its final marginal cost applies to all 20 miles.
The budget is insufficient because the $800 million added benefit must also be paid as cost.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
legendaryBoss.feedback: MC rises from $20 million to $30 million per mile, so added cost is 20 x (20 + 30)/2 = $500 million. MSB falls from 50 to 30, giving added benefit 20 x (50 + 30)/2 = $800 million. Net gain is $300 million.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Coastal flood protection graph with downward-sloping MSB and upward-sloping MC intersecting at 30 miles and $30 million per mile.
legendaryBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is miles of coastal flood protection. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in millions of dollars per mile. MSB equals 60 minus Q and MC equals 15 plus 0.5Q. They intersect at 30 miles, where both equal $30 million per mile.

legendaryBoss.q: Refer to the fireworks graph and treat displays as continuous. Suppose a proposal uses only North’s willingness to pay to decide provision. What quantity and welfare loss result compared with using both neighborhoods’ benefits, ignoring funding costs?
options: Four displays and no welfare loss, because the larger neighborhood represents everyone.
Zero displays and $200,000 of forgone net benefits, equal to the full cost of four displays.
Eight displays and $20,000 of forgone benefits, because neighborhood quantities should be added.
Zero displays and $80,000 of forgone net benefits.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
legendaryBoss.feedback: North MB equals MC only at Q = 0 and is below MC for positive quantities. Summed MSB starts $40,000 above MC and meets MC at Q = 4. Omitting all four displays loses the triangle 0.5 x 4 x 40,000 = $80,000.
legendaryBoss.imageAlt: Community fireworks graph with North MB, South MB, vertically summed MSB, and MC, with decomposition guides at four displays.
legendaryBoss.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is community fireworks displays per summer. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in thousands of dollars per display. North MB is max of zero and 50 minus 5Q. South MB is max of zero and 40 minus 5Q. MSB is their vertical sum and MC equals $50,000 per display. At four displays, North MB is $30,000, South MB is $20,000, and MSB equals MC at $50,000.

repairQuestions.q: An externality is:
options: A cost or benefit affecting a third party outside the transaction.
Any change in the market price.
A government expenditure.
A cost paid fully by the buyer.
repairQuestions.commonError: Calling every market effect an externality.
repairQuestions.feedback: Externalities spill over to people not directly involved in the exchange.

repairQuestions.q: What makes an effect an externality?
options: It spills onto a third party outside the transaction
The outcome is a public good by definition
A large firm merely changes its own cost
The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
repairQuestions.commonError: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
repairQuestions.feedback: An externality affects people outside the transaction.

repairQuestions.q: A public good is defined by:
options: Government ownership alone.
Nonrival consumption and difficulty excluding nonpayers.
A high market price.
Private benefits only.
repairQuestions.commonError: Using the provider rather than the good’s characteristics.
repairQuestions.feedback: Public-good status depends on rivalry and excludability.

repairQuestions.q: Which question should a student ask first when deciding whether a service is excludable?
options: How many firms sell it?
Does government approve it?
Can nonpayers feasibly be prevented from receiving it?
Is its total benefit positive?
repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing excludability with legal prohibition rather than the feasibility of denying access to nonpayers.
repairQuestions.feedback: Excludability is about feasible denial of access to nonpayers, not legality, supplier competition, or total social benefit.

repairQuestions.q: A shared resource is described as rival. What evidence would support that description?
options: Each user's consumption leaves less quantity or quality for others
Users can be charged a membership fee
Several suppliers advertise it
The resource is socially valuable
repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing rivalry with competition instead of asking whether one person's use reduces what remains for others.
repairQuestions.feedback: Rival consumption means one user's activity reduces the quantity or quality available to other users.

repairQuestions.q: A student says free riding means 'people are bad.' What is the more precise economic explanation?
options: Public goods eliminate incentives
Free riding requires theft
Nonrivalry means only one person benefits
Nonexcludability allows a person to benefit without bearing the contribution cost
repairQuestions.commonError: Treating free riding as simple selfishness rather than an incentive created by nonexcludability.
repairQuestions.feedback: The mechanism is an incentive created by nonexcludability: an individual can receive the benefit while shifting payment to others.

repairQuestions.q: What is the precise private-provision concern for a pure nonexcludable public good?
options: Private firms are legally barred from production
Market revenue may fall short of the social value created
Marginal social benefit is always zero
Every unit is overused like a common resource
repairQuestions.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
repairQuestions.feedback: When beneficiaries can receive the good without paying, the provider cannot capture all willingness to pay, so profitable output may be below efficient provision.

repairQuestions.q: How does market power differ from an externality?
options: Market power requires a third-party spillover outside the transaction
It influences market terms rather than imposing a third-party spillover
Market power makes the good nonrival and nonexcludable
Market power occurs only when income is distributed unequally.
repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
repairQuestions.feedback: Market power can restrict mutually beneficial trades by influencing price or quantity.

bridgeQuestions.q: Pollution changes a firm’s private marginal choice. What connection matters?
options: The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
Marginal analysis can compare private and social cost
The outcome is a public good by definition
A large firm merely changes its own cost
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Marginal analysis compares the private marginal incentives facing the firm with the social marginal cost that includes the pollution spillover.

bridgeQuestions.q: A shared office kitchen is repeatedly left dirty because each worker expects others to clean it. This resembles:
options: A common-resource or collective-action problem.
A perfectly enforced private property right.
A positive price signal.
A competitive firm’s shutdown decision.
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Failing to transfer shared-resource incentives to everyday settings.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Shared access and dispersed responsibility can encourage overuse or under-maintenance.

bridgeQuestions.q: A public-good rule changes incentives to contribute. What connection matters?
options: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
It is rival with fully enforceable private access
Free-riding incentives can reduce voluntary provision
It is a private good supplied by government
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Because nonpayers can still benefit from a public good, contribution rules affect free-riding incentives and therefore voluntary provision.

bridgeQuestions.q: A free public beach becomes crowded enough that each visitor has less space. What changed?
options: The beach became excludable without an access rule
Consumption became rival at the congested level
Firm rivalry increased
Nonpayers became easier to identify automatically
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Crowding means another visitor reduces the quality or space available to others, so use becomes rival even though access remains difficult to exclude.

bridgeQuestions.q: A paid satellite weather feed can deny access to noncustomers and can serve another subscriber without using up the forecast. What is it?
options: Club good
Public good
Private good
Common resource
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Encryption makes the feed excludable and the information is nonrival over the stated range, so it is a club good.

bridgeQuestions.q: A common resource is being overused. What is the key private-social gap?
options: Users omit all of their own benefit
The resource is nonrival
The supplier cannot calculate marginal revenue
Users omit part of the depletion or congestion cost imposed on others
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Calling any shared problem a tragedy of the commons without establishing rivalry and difficult exclusion.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Open-access users capture much of their private benefit but do not bear the full cost their rival use imposes on others.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can property or access rights improve common-resource efficiency?
options: They make the resource nonrival
They guarantee zero transaction cost
They remove every competing use
They make users bear more of the opportunity cost of depletion
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assuming ownership alone guarantees efficiency without clear, enforceable rights and feasible monitoring.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Enforceable rights connect current use with forgone future value or lost use by others, reducing the incentive for open-access overuse.

failure_recognition.q: Pollution changes a firm’s private marginal choice. What connection matters?
options: The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
Marginal analysis can compare private and social cost
The outcome is a public good by definition
A large firm merely changes its own cost
failure_recognition.commonError: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
failure_recognition.feedback: Marginal analysis compares the private marginal incentives facing the firm with the social marginal cost that includes the pollution spillover.

failure_recognition.q: A shared office kitchen is repeatedly left dirty because each worker expects others to clean it. This resembles:
options: A common-resource or collective-action problem.
A perfectly enforced private property right.
A positive price signal.
A competitive firm’s shutdown decision.
failure_recognition.commonError: Failing to transfer shared-resource incentives to everyday settings.
failure_recognition.feedback: Shared access and dispersed responsibility can encourage overuse or under-maintenance.

failure_recognition.q: A public-good rule changes incentives to contribute. What connection matters?
options: It is nonrival but easy to exclude
It is rival with fully enforceable private access
Free-riding incentives can reduce voluntary provision
It is a private good supplied by government
failure_recognition.commonError: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
failure_recognition.feedback: Because nonpayers can still benefit from a public good, contribution rules affect free-riding incentives and therefore voluntary provision.

easy.q: A voluntary coffee purchase makes both participants better off. Does this show market failure?
options: No; mutually accepted trade alone identifies no efficiency wedge
Yes; buyers and sellers always have unequal power
Yes; every price excludes some consumers
No; market failure requires government ownership
easy.commonError: Calling every disliked, unequal, or expensive outcome a market failure.
easy.feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

easy.q: Pollution from a factory that harms nearby residents is an example of:
options: A price floor
A negative externality
A perfectly efficient market
A positive externality.
easy.commonError: confuses_externality_with_private_cost
easy.feedback: Pollution affects bystanders, so it is a negative externality.

easy.q: A public good is usually:
options: Always sold by one monopoly firm
A legal maximum price
Hard to exclude people from and shared by many users
A substitute for every other good
easy.commonError: confuses_public_good_with_government_provided_good
easy.feedback: Public goods are generally nonexcludable and nonrival.

easy.q: A seller with substantial influence over the market price has:
options: A price ceiling
A PPF
A circular flow
Market power
easy.commonError: confuses_market_power_with_high_demand
easy.feedback: Market power exists when a buyer or seller can influence price.

easy.q: Which situation is most likely a market failure?
options: A factory pollutes a river used by nearby households
A buyer voluntarily purchases coffee
A seller lowers price during a sale
A student chooses to study
easy.commonError: thinks_any_unwanted_outcome_is_market_failure
easy.feedback: Pollution that harms third parties is a market failure because the full cost is not reflected in the market.

easy.q: A neighbor bears smoke from a restaurant exhaust fan. What feature identifies an externality?
options: The outcome is a public good by definition
A third party bears a cost outside the transaction
A large firm merely changes its own cost
The effect falls only on the buyer and seller
easy.commonError: Calling an effect on a buyer or seller a third-party spillover.
easy.feedback: An externality affects people outside the transaction.

easy.q: A storm-warning signal can serve another listener without reducing its value and nonpayers are hard to exclude. What is it?
options: It is rival with fully enforceable private access
It is a private good supplied by government
A public good
It is nonrival but easy to exclude
easy.commonError: Confusing public goods with common resources or government-provided goods.
easy.feedback: Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude.

easy.q: A seller can profitably influence price by restricting output. What concern appears?
options: A negative externality imposed on third parties
A public-good free-rider problem
A common-resource overuse problem.
Market power
easy.commonError: Confusing market power with an externality or merely a large firm.
easy.feedback: Market power can restrict mutually beneficial trades by influencing price or quantity.

easy.q: Refer to the fast-fashion garments graph. Which type of externality is represented by the private and social marginal curves?
options: Negative production externality
Negative consumption externality
Positive production externality
Positive consumption externality
easy.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
easy.feedback: This is a negative production externality: the activity creates a cost for people outside the market transaction, so the relevant social and private marginal curves differ.

easy.q: Based on the fast-fashion garments graph, what economic relationship explains the position of the social curve relative to the private curve?
options: MSC is below MPC because buyers receive an external benefit
MSC is above MPC because production imposes an external cost
MPB is above MSB because production creates a benefit
MPC is above MSC because firms pay every social cost
easy.commonError: Using private curves alone when social costs or benefits determine efficiency.
easy.feedback: MSC is above MPC because production imposes an external cost. The constant vertical separation is the marginal external cost omitted from private decisions.

easy.q: If no corrective policy is adopted, how will the market quantity of fast-fashion garments compare with the socially efficient quantity?
options: The market underproduces by 80 million garments
The market is efficient because MPB intersects MPC
The market overproduces by 80 million garments
The market overproduces by 160 million garments
easy.commonError: Using private curves alone when social costs or benefits determine efficiency.
easy.feedback: The unregulated market equilibrium occurs where MPC intersects MPB, at 240 million garments and $12. The socially efficient outcome occurs where MSC intersects MPB, at 160 million garments and $15. The difference is 80 million garments, so the market has overproduction. Private choices omit the external cost.

easy.q: A steel mill's smoke harms nearby households. Which classification is most precise?
options: Negative production externality
Negative consumption externality
Positive production externality
Positive consumption externality
easy.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
easy.feedback: Production imposes a third-party cost. Because the smoke is created during production, the omitted harm raises marginal social cost above the mill's private marginal cost.

easy.q: Secondhand smoke from using a product harms restaurant patrons. What kind of spillover is this?
options: Negative production externality
Negative consumption externality
Positive production externality
Positive consumption externality
easy.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
easy.feedback: The harmful spillover follows consumption. The purchase itself is not the spillover; the harm generated when the product is consumed falls on people outside the transaction.

easy.q: A beekeeper's hives improve nearby orchard yields without payment. How is the effect classified?
options: Negative production externality
Negative consumption externality
Positive production externality
Positive consumption externality
easy.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
easy.feedback: Production by the beekeeper creates an external benefit. The beekeeper does not capture all of the added orchard output, so the social benefit of producing hives exceeds the private benefit.

easy.q: A vaccination reduces infection risk for people other than the patient. What is the spillover?
options: Negative consumption externality
Negative production externality
Positive production externality
Positive consumption externality
easy.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
easy.feedback: Consuming the vaccination benefits third parties. The patient receives a private benefit, while reduced transmission creates an additional social benefit for other people.

easy.q: A landscaping company creates noise while serving a customer. Which channel creates the externality?
options: Production
Consumption
A public-good channel
A price-control channel
easy.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
easy.feedback: The spillover is created while the service is produced. The customer and landscaper are the transacting parties, while nearby residents experience a cost created by the production process.

easy.q: A driver's use of a congested road delays other drivers. Which description is best?
options: A positive production externality
A negative consumption externality
A private cost borne only by the driver
A positive consumption externality
easy.commonError: Misclassifying the sign or the production-versus-consumption channel of an externality.
easy.feedback: Road use imposes delay on other users. Each trip adds congestion delays for other road users, so the driver's private cost understates the social cost of road use.

easy.q: A rule requires factories to install a verified scrubber. What policy type is this?
options: A corrective consumer subsidy
A tradable-permit market
Command-and-control technology regulation
A private Coase bargain
easy.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
easy.feedback: The rule mandates a technology. Because the regulator specifies the equipment rather than a price or emissions allowance, firms cannot choose a different compliance technology.

easy.q: A city caps each plant's sulfur emissions at 20 tons. What instrument is used?
options: A consumption subsidy
An unregulated permit market
A price floor on output
An emissions standard
easy.commonError: Treating every regulation as equivalent or ignoring the efficient quantity target.
easy.feedback: A legal maximum emissions amount is a standard. The legal maximum directly constrains each plant's emissions quantity; it does not create a subsidy or a tradable right by itself.

easy.q: Education benefits employers and neighbors beyond the student. What quantity tendency can result?
options: Underconsumption relative to social optimum
Overconsumption
No efficiency effect
A binding price floor
easy.commonError: Reversing social and private curves or predicting overproduction instead of underproduction.
easy.feedback: Private marginal benefit can lie below social marginal benefit. Because consumers count only their private return, MPB lies below MSB and the private market stops before all socially worthwhile units are consumed.

easy.q: A per-unit subsidy equals vaccination's marginal external benefit. What is intended?
options: Reduce vaccination below market quantity
Leave private incentives unchanged
Increase vaccination toward socially efficient quantity
Turn benefit into external cost
easy.commonError: Confusing subsidy expenditure with external benefit or taxing a positive externality.
easy.feedback: The subsidy raises private incentive by the external benefit. By rewarding the external benefit, the subsidy raises the consumer's effective private incentive and moves the MPB-based choice toward the MSB-based efficient quantity.

easy.q: Why is it too strong to claim that private firms can never participate in public-radio provision?
options: Advertising, contracts, donations, or government purchasing can create revenue
Nonexcludability guarantees subscription revenue
MC disappears for private firms
Private Benefit must always equal MSB
easy.commonError: Claiming private firms never participate instead of identifying the payment problem for a pure nonexcludable public good.
easy.feedback: Alternative institutions can finance private participation even when direct listener payments understate social benefit. The underprovision result is conditional, not a claim that private participation is impossible.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At 20 miles of coastal protection, which marginal comparison is correct?
options: MSB exceeds MC, so expanding protection raises net social benefit
MC exceeds MSB, so protection should contract
MSB equals MC, so 20 miles is efficient
Private Benefit is necessarily zero
easy.commonError: Treating rivalry as firm competition or assuming a good's category cannot change with access rules or congestion.
easy.feedback: At Q = 20, the graph shows MSB at $40 million and MC at $25 million. The next mile adds more benefit than cost.
easy.imageAlt: Coastal flood protection graph with downward-sloping MSB and upward-sloping MC intersecting at 30 miles and $30 million per mile.
easy.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is miles of coastal flood protection. The vertical axis is marginal benefit and marginal cost in millions of dollars per mile. MSB equals 60 minus Q and MC equals 15 plus 0.5Q. They intersect at 30 miles, where both equal $30 million per mile.

easy.q: Community-wide coastal protection can serve another resident without reducing protection for anyone else. Which characteristic does that illustrate?
options: Each protected resident removes protection from another
Only one buyer can consume each mile
Many residents receive the same protection without using it up
Open harvesting depletes the barrier
easy.commonError: Classifying from who supplies the good instead of the stated excludability and rivalry conditions.
easy.feedback: Flood protection is nonrival over the stated range because protecting another resident does not subtract protection from others.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. At four displays, what marginal social benefit results from vertically summing North and South?

easy.feedback: At Q = 4, North MB is $30,000 and South MB is $20,000. Because both consume the same display, the benefits add vertically to MSB of $50,000.

At four displays, North MB is $30,000, South MB is $20,000, and MSB equals MC at $50,000.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Which calculation would misread the shared quantity at 40 hours?
options: Adding Group A's 40 hours to Group B's 40 hours to claim 80 hours
Adding marginal benefits of $3,000 and $1,000
Reporting MSB of $4,000 per hour
Recognizing both groups receive 40 hours

easy.feedback: Public-good beneficiaries share one common quantity. Their marginal benefits are added vertically; their identical consumed quantities are not added together.
